It appears in the account where the Ark of the Covenant, captured by the Philistines, is returned to Israel: the cart carrying it stops in the field of Joshua of Beth-Schémesch, and the inhabitants offer the cows as a burnt offering to the Lord (1 Samuel 6:14).
2. An inhabitant of Beth-Schémesch is called a Bethschémésch or Beth-Schémeschite. These inhabitants are mentioned in relation to the return of the ark (1 Samuel 6:18).
H1030.origine: The Hebrew name בֵּית־הַשִּׁמְשִׁי (bet hash-shimshi) comes from בֵּית ("house") and שֶׁ֫מֶשׁ ("sun"). It is an adjectival or patronymic form designating either the city itself or the inhabitant who is from there. The city of Beth-Schémesch bears this name due to its worship or its geography related to the sun in ancient Levantine culture.
H1030.emploi: Beth-Schémesch appears twice in the first book of Samuel, both in chapter 6, during the miraculous return of the Ark of the Covenant after its capture by the Philistines. It is a key location in the geographical relief of ancient Israel, known as an important center in the region of Judea. The biblical mentions place it in a context of worship and restoration of the relationship between Israel and its God after a national humiliation.
H1030.portee: The account of Beth-Schémesch shows how God brings back His ark to Israel and claims His people after a defeat. This city becomes a witness to a divine salvific act: it receives the ark and its inhabitants recognize the hand of God. It is a call for the reader to see in historical events the presence and sovereignty of God over His people.

sens: Location in the territory of Benjamin, situated at the border with Judah
H1031.detail: Beth-Hogla is a city mentioned three times in the book of Joshua, regarding the division of the lands among the tribes of Israel. It served as a landmark to mark the borders: it appears in the description of the boundary between Judah and Benjamin (Joshua 15:6), then as a marker of the southern boundary of the territory of Benjamin (Joshua 18:19), and finally in the list of cities that belonged to Benjamin (Joshua 18:21). Its location near the Jordan and the Dead Sea placed it in the Jordan Valley, a low and fertile area.
H1031.origine: The name Beth-Hogla literally means "house of the partridge" or "place of the partridge" in Hebrew: beth means "house" or "place," and hoglah refers to the partridge, a common migratory bird in the Holy Land. The name thus evokes either a location known for the abundance of these birds or a place named after a memorable event or natural feature.
H1031.emploi: Beth-Hogla is mentioned only in the book of Joshua at the time of the land division. It first appears in the list of the borders of Judah (15:6), then in that of Benjamin (18:19 and 18:21). It served as a geographical marker to establish the territorial limits between two tribes, indicating that it was a site easily identifiable and recognizable, likely an important passage point in the region.

sens: Fortified city in the mountains of Ephraim
Strategic battle and pursuit location
City assigned to the Levites
H1032G.detail:
1. Beth-Horon refers to two twin cities located in the mountains of Ephraim, one at a higher elevation (Upper Beth-Horon) and the other lower (Lower Beth-Horon), with a difference of about 245 meters in elevation. The road connecting them is a strategic passage in the geography of Canaan.

2. The city is famous as the site of a decisive victory for Israel: after the battle of Gibeon, the Lord routed the Canaanite kings, and Israel pursued them "on the road that goes up to Beth-Horon" (Joshua 10:10), and even the Lord caused large hailstones to fall on the fleeing enemies (Joshua 10:11).

3. Beth-Horon also served as a military route for armies: Saul and his army passed through this road during their tactical movements (1 Samuel 13:18).

4. After the conquest, Beth-Horon was assigned to the Levites as a city of refuge and residence (Joshua 21:22; 1 Chronicles 6:68), showing its lasting importance in the territory of Israel.
H1032G.origine: The name literally means "house of the hollow" or "house of the void," probably referring to the topography: the area is characterized by hollow valleys and mountainous passages. This geographical name reflects the terrain configuration, evident in the biblical usages where Beth-Horon is always associated with roads, ascents, and passages between heights.
H1032G.emploi: Beth-Horon appears seven times in the historical books (Joshua, 1 Samuel, 1 Chronicles). It is first known as the site of the most spectacular military victory of Israel after entering Canaan: Joshua 10:10-11 recounts how the Canaanite army was pursued and struck down on this road, with the miraculous intervention of the Lord who caused hail to fall. It is then mentioned as a geographical landmark (Joshua 18:14), as a Levitical city (Joshua 21:22; 1 Chronicles 6:68), and as a passage route for Israelite armies (1 Samuel 13:18). Beth-Horon symbolizes the permanent presence of Israel in the mountains of Ephraim after the conquest.
H1032G.portee: Beth-Horon reminds us how God defends Israel and grants victory not by brute force, but by His direct intervention. The passage of large hailstones shows that the battle belongs to the Lord. For the Christian, this place evokes the sovereignty of God over historical events and the courage to trust His promises in decisive moments.

sens: Location in the hill country of Ephraim, in the Promised Land
H1032H.detail: 1. Beth-Horon is a city located in the heights of Ephraim, in Canaan. Its name literally means "house of the cavity" or "house of the hollow," perhaps evoking the mountainous terrain characterized by valleys. It exists in two versions: Upper Beth-Horon and Lower Beth-Horon, situated close to each other on the same ridge.
H1032H.origine: The Hebrew name בֵּית חוֹרֹן ("Beït Horon") combines בֵּית ("house," the dwelling or place) and חוֹרֹן ("Horon"), whose etymology refers to the idea of hollow or cavity, possibly in reference to natural caves or the rugged terrain of the mountainous area. This type of geographical name was common in Canaan, designating places by their prominent physical characteristics.
H1032H.emploi: Beth-Horon is mentioned twice in the Bible. In Joshua 16:5, it appears as the eastern boundary of the land inheritance of the tribe of Ephraim, marking the border of the territory assigned to this tribe during the conquest of Canaan. In 2 Chronicles 8:5, King Solomon fortifies it by building or strengthening Upper Beth-Horon and Lower Beth-Horon as fortified cities, equipped with walls, gates, and bars, demonstrating its strategic importance in the defense of the territory.

sens: Fortified city in the hill country of Ephraim, in ancient Palestine
The Lower: locality situated 245 meters lower than the Upper, to the west
H1032I.detail:
1. Beth-Horon is an important city in the hill country of Ephraim, in the Promised Land. Its name means "house of the cavity" or "house of the hollow," likely evoking the geographical features of the place — perhaps caves or rugged terrain. The city appears as a strategic point in the territory of Judah and Ephraim (Joshua 16:3; Joshua 18:13).

2. Beth-Horon existed in two settlements: the Upper and the Lower. The Lower was located about 245 meters lower than the Upper, on the western slopes of the mountain. King Solomon and his lineage fortified these two cities with walls, gates, and bars, making them strongholds to control access (1 Kings 9:17; 2 Chronicles 8:5). The daughter of Manasseh, Sheerah, participated in their construction (1 Chronicles 7:24).
H1032I.origine: The Hebrew name בֵּית חוֹרֹן (Beth-Horon) is composed of בֵּית ("house") and חוֹרֹן, which likely means "hollow" or "cavity." This etymology suggests a place characterized by hollow geological formations, caves, or valleys. The dual name (Upper and Lower Beth-Horon) indicates two related settlements located at different altitudes on the same mountainous area.
H1032I.emploi: Beth-Horon appears five times in the Bible, always as a fortified city. It first appears in the descriptions of the borders of the territories of Ephraim and Benjamin (Joshua 16:3 and 18:13), then in the account of the military consolidation of the kingdom under Solomon, who rebuilt or strengthened Lower Beth-Horon (1 Kings 9:17; 2 Chronicles 8:5). One mention shows that the daughter of Manasseh also contributed to its construction (1 Chronicles 7:24). These references always present it as a strategic stronghold, never as a simple village.
H1032I.portee: Beth-Horon symbolizes the consolidation of Israelite power and control over the heights of the Promised Land. Its fortification under Solomon illustrates how God provided His people with strong cities for their protection and rest after the wars of conquest. For the reader, this city serves as a reminder that God ensures not only victory but also the lasting security of His people.

sens: Place in the territory of the Philistines
H1033.detail: Beth-Car is a location in Canaan that was situated within the influence or territory of the Philistines. The name literally means "house of the ram" or "dwelling of the ram" — an evocative name, likely given because the place was notable for the presence of rams or had the shape of a fortified enclosure. It was at this location that the army of Israel, under the leadership of Samuel, pursued and defeated the Philistines in a decisive battle (1 Samuel 7:11).
H1033.origine: The name Beth-Car is composed of two Hebrew words: "beth" (בֵּית) meaning "house" or "dwelling" and "kar" (כָּר) meaning "ram." It is a typical place name in Canaan, formed according to the model "house of + animal or thing," common in ancient Semitic geography.
H1033.emploi: Beth-Car appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 7:11. It is there that the text reports how the men of Israel, after consulting the Lord through Samuel and confessing their sins, defeated the Philistine army that was invading their land. This was a turning point: the victory halted the enemy's advance and marked a moment of deliverance for Israel.

sens: City in the territory of Simeon
Locality in ancient Palestine
H1034.detail: Beth-Lebaoth is a city that belonged to the territory of the tribe of Simeon in the Promised Land. Its Hebrew name literally means "house of lionesses," perhaps suggesting a place known for the presence of lions or an evocative name given to a stronghold. It is mentioned in the enumeration of cities in the territory of Simeon (Joshua 19:6).
H1034.origine: The name Beth-Lebaoth is composed of two Hebrew words: "beth" (house) and "lebaoth" (lionesses, feminine plural of lion). This type of place name, starting with "beth," is common in the Promised Land (Bethlehem, Bethel, etc.). The meaning evokes strength and power associated with lions.
H1034.emploi: Beth-Lebaoth appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:6, in the context of the division of lands among the tribes of Israel. It is listed among the thirteen cities assigned to the tribe of Simeon. It is a little-known biblical geographical landmark, mentioned only to establish the borders of the territory of Simeon.

sens: City of Judah, located near Jerusalem
Birthplace of King David
Famous city for its inhabitants and rural life
H1035G.detail:
1. Bethlehem is a city located in Judah, on the road to Ephrath. Its name literally means "house of bread," which evokes the agricultural abundance and fertility of the region. Naomi and Ruth arrive there during the barley harvest, finding refuge and sustenance in this city (Ruth 1:19-22).

2. Bethlehem became famous as the birthplace of David. Samuel goes there to anoint David among the sons of Jesse, a man from Bethlehem who tended his flocks there (1 Samuel 16:4; 1 Samuel 17:15). It is from this city that the future king of Israel emerges.

3. Bethlehem held an important place in the life of the Judah clans: it welcomed dispersed inhabitants and was known for its quality citizens. Judges of Israel lived there, and the bravest warriors of David had their roots there, such as the one who drew water from the well of Bethlehem at the risk of his life (2 Samuel 23:16; 1 Chronicles 11:17).
H1035G.origine: The Hebrew name בֵּית לֶחֶם (bet lechem) literally means "house of bread": בֵּית (bet) = house, and לֶחֶם (lechem) = bread. This designation reflects the abundance of wheat and food that characterized this fertile region of Judah. The word יְלִדוּ (they gave birth) shows that Bethlehem was a center of family and agricultural life, and it became in the Bible the symbol of the birthplace of kings and saviors.
H1035G.emploi: Bethlehem appears 38 times in the Bible, mainly in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and in the books of Ruth and Judges. It is first mentioned as a burial landmark where Rachel was buried (Genesis 35:19), then becomes the center of the story of Ruth, a foreign woman who finds refuge there and marries Boaz. Bethlehem is then inseparable from the story of David: it is where he is born, where he is anointed by Samuel, and where he returns to tend the flocks before becoming king. His most faithful warriors are rooted there. The city also appears in the lists of populations upon return from exile, and the prophet Micah identifies it as the place from which the Messiah will come (Micah 5:1).
H1035G.portee: Bethlehem reveals how God works through ordinary places. A small agricultural town becomes the cradle of the king who will save Israel. For the Christian, Bethlehem speaks of the humility of the origins of salvation: not in a great capital, but in a house of bread, a simple place of sustenance. The story of Ruth in Bethlehem shows how divine providence welcomes the foreigner and the poor. This city anchors the divine promise in the concrete geography of the chosen people.

sens: City of the tribe of Zebulun in Israel
H1035H.detail: Bethlehem is a small town located in the territory of the tribe of Zebulun, in northern Galilee. It is named in the list of the twelve cities of Zebulun (Joshua 19:15), where it appears between Nahalal and Shimron. Its name means "house of bread" in Hebrew, which likely evokes the fertility of its region.
H1035H.origine: The name Bethlehem literally means "house of bread": "beit" (house) and "lechem" (bread, food). This name designates a prosperous agricultural place. It should not be confused with Bethlehem of Judea, the birthplace of Jesus, which is much more famous in biblical history.
H1035H.emploi: Bethlehem of Zebulun appears only once in the Bible, during the division of the land promised to the tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan. It is simply listed among the fortified cities assigned to Zebulun (Joshua 19:15), with no particular event associated with it in the preserved biblical texts.

sens: Palestinian city mentioned in a prophetic oracle
H1036.detail: Acco is a Palestinian city, capital of the Philistines according to some ancient traditions. The name literally means "house of Aphrah" or "house of dust." The Bible mentions it in Micah 1:10, where the prophet plays on the names of Philistine cities to express the mourning and humiliation of the people: "I roll in the dust at Beth Leaphra" — this dust evokes both the name of the city ("dust") and the act of mourning by rolling on the ground.
H1036.origine: The Hebrew word בֵּית לְעַפְרָה (Beit-le-Aphrah) is composed of בֵּית ("house") and עַפְרָה ("Aphrah"), whose root הח (aph) denotes dust. It is a geographical name, probably a variant or an ancient name for Ophrah, a Palestinian city.
H1036.emploi: Acco appears only once in the Segond 1910, in Micah 1:10. It is a prophetic oracle where Micah lists several Palestinian cities and plays on their names to announce desolation. The context is that of divine judgment on the Philistines and the oppression of Israel. This unique mention shows that the city was known in biblical times as an important Philistine possession.
H1036.portee: This city name invites the reader to meditate on God's judgment that reaches the nations opposed to His people. The wordplay between the name Acco ("dust") and the image of mourning — rolling in the dust — reminds us that even earthly powers will be humiliated before divine will.

sens: Fortress or fortified bastion near Shechem
Place of gathering and political power
Site of acts of violence and betrayal
H1037.detail:
1. Millo refers to a fortified structure, probably a bastion or rampart, located near the city of Shechem in Canaan. The name literally means "house of the rampart" or "house of the fortress." It is a strategic location that served as a local stronghold.

2. Millo is presented as a center of political and social power. In Judges 9:6, all the inhabitants of Shechem and "the house of Millo" gather to proclaim Abimelech king — it is a place where major decisions affecting the city are made.

3. Millo is also the scene of violence and conspiracies. In 2 Kings 12:20, King Joash is assassinated there by his servants who "formed a conspiracy" — this bastion becomes the site of a bloody betrayal against the sovereign.
H1037.origine: The Hebrew name "Beit Millo" literally means "house of Millo" or "house of the rampart." The word "millo" (מִלּוֹא) evokes a fortification, a wall, or a bastion. It is a place-name that has retained its name through the centuries, designating a particular fortified site.
H1037.emploi: Millo appears three times in the Bible, each time in an important political or military context. In Judges 9:6, it is the place where the citizens of Shechem gather to crown Abimelech, marking a major political act — a royal proclamation. Verse 20 of the same chapter associates it with a curse pronounced by Jotham, who calls down fire to destroy both Abimelech and the house of Millo, thus linking them in the same judgment. In 2 Kings 12:20, several centuries later, Millo reappears as the place where King Joash is assassinated during a conspiracy, placing this bastion at the heart of a political drama. The place remains a symbol of power, but also of violence and betrayal.
H1037.portee: For the reader, Millo reminds us that even places of power and political authority are subject to God's judgment. The succession of events — contested coronation, pronounced curse, royal assassination — shows how God governs the history of men and how sin and betrayal have their consequences. This proper name invites reflection on the fragility of human institutions when they turn away from God.

sens: Fortified city of Transjordan
Location in the territory of Gad
H1039.detail: Beth-Nimra is a fortified city mentioned twice in the Bible, both times in relation to the conquest and division of the lands east of the Jordan. Its name means "house of the panther" or "house of the leopard," likely referring to the animal that roamed the area. The city was located in the territory allotted to the tribe of Gad during the division of Canaan after the Exodus.
H1039.origine: The name Beth-Nimra combines two Hebrew words: "Beit" (בֵּית) meaning "house" or "place of," and "Nimrah" (נִמְרָה) referring to the panther or leopard. This type of geographical name composed with "Beit" (Bethlehem, Bethel, etc.) is common in Hebrew. The name reveals the characteristic fauna of the region or may refer to a particular feature of the place associated with this predator.
H1039.emploi: Beth-Nimra appears twice in the Bible, both in the context of the settlement of the tribes in Transjordan. In Numbers 32:36, it is listed among the strong cities that the descendants of Gad and Reuben built or fortified to protect their flocks. In Joshua 13:27, it is mentioned in the description of the borders of the territory of Gad, locating the city in the valley, east of the Jordan, alongside other locations such as Beth-Haram and Succoth. These two passages highlight its strategic and administrative importance in the territorial organization of the tribes east of the Jordan.

sens: City of ancient Syria
H1040.detail: Bith-Éden is a city located in ancient Syria, in the region of Upper Mesopotamia. The name literally means "house of delight" or "house of beauty." It is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Amos 1:5, where the prophet announces divine judgment against the Arameans of Damascus.
H1040.origine: The name Bith-Éden means "house of delight," combining the Hebrew word "bêt" (house) and "éden" (delight, paradise). It is the same word used to refer to the Garden of Eden. Non-biblical historical sources, including Assyrian cuneiform inscriptions, identify it with the ancient city of Bit Adini, a prosperous Aramean city-state located in present-day northern Syria, near the Euphrates River.
H1040.emploi: Bith-Éden appears only once in the Bible, in Amos 1:5. The prophet Amos lists the judgments that God will pronounce against the neighboring nations of Israel. Concerning the Arameans of Damascus, he declares that God will break the gate of Damascus and that "the inhabitants of Syria will be taken captive to Kir." Bith-Éden is mentioned as one of the cities of this kingdom that divine judgment will strike, marking the political collapse of Aramean power in the face of Assyria.

sens: Location near Jerusalem
Place of residence for a Jewish community upon return from exile
H1041.detail:
1. Beth-Azmaveth is a village located near Jerusalem, in the region of Judea. Its Hebrew name literally means "house of the strength of death": a classic Hebrew expression to designate a place rather than a mere accumulation of words.
2. Upon returning from exile in Babylon, this village housed Jewish families who resettled there. In the census of Nehemiah 7:28, forty-two inhabitants of Beth-Azmaveth are counted among those returning from captivity and settling in the holy land.
H1041.origine: Beth-Azmaveth comes from two Hebrew words: "beth" (בֵּית), meaning "house" or "place," and "Azmaveth" (עַזְמָ֫וֶת), meaning "strength of death." This locality shares the same name as the person mentioned in 2 Samuel 23:31, one of David's warriors, although the link between them is uncertain. The geographical name was well established in the region of Benjamin before and after the exile.
H1041.emploi: Beth-Azmaveth appears only once in the preserved Bible, in Nehemiah 7:28. It is listed among the cities whose inhabitants returned from captivity in Babylon and resettled in Judea. This context suggests that it was a fortified or significant locality in the region of Benjamin, populated enough for the text to specifically note the number of its inhabitants (forty-two) at the time of the return.

sens: City in the territory of Judah
H1042.detail: Beth-Anoth is a small locality in the kingdom of Judah, listed among the cities in the territory that was allotted to the tribe of Judah after the conquest of Canaan. It appears in the list of southern Judah cities alongside Maarath and Elthekon (Joshua 15:59).
H1042.origine: The name Beth-Anoth literally means "house of answers" or "house of afflictions" in Hebrew: Beit ("house") and Anoth ("answers" or "afflictions"). Like many place names in Israel, this name evokes a notable feature of the site, either a sanctuary or a place associated with prayers and divine responses, or a location linked to suffering or mourning.
H1042.emploi: Beth-Anoth is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:59. It appears in the long enumeration of cities and villages allotted to Judah during the division of the territory among the tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan. This list shows the extent of Judah's possessions and the administrative organization of the kingdom.

sens: City allotted to the tribe of Naphtali
Place where the Canaanites were not driven out but subjected to tribute
H1043.detail:
1. Beth-Anath is a city in Galilee, located in the territory of the tribe of Naphtali. It is listed among the cities allotted to this tribe during the division of the land after the conquest (Joshua 19:38), alongside Jireon, Migdal-El, and Horem.
2. Unlike other conquests, the Canaanite inhabitants of Beth-Anath were not expelled: the tribe of Naphtali only subjected them to the payment of tribute (Judges 1:33). This is one of the examples of compromise between Israel and the local populations during the settlement period.
H1043.origine: The name literally means "house of response" or "house of affliction" (from the Hebrew "house" and the divine name Anat, Canaanite goddess). Although the Bible attributes this city to Israel, its name reflects its Canaanite origins.
H1043.emploi: Beth-Anath appears only twice in the Bible, both in connection with Naphtali. First mentioned among the cities of the lot of Naphtali (Joshua 19:38), it reappears in the account of incomplete conquests: the tribe did not establish its total dominance there but imposed tribute on the Canaanites (Judges 1:33). It illustrates a particular moment in Israel's history where the settlement in the land was not total and definitive.
H1043.portee: Beth-Anath reminds us that the conquest of the promised land was progressive and imperfect. This city shows the limits of faith and obedience: rather than completely driving out the Canaanites as God commanded, the Israelites chose an easier arrangement. It serves as a warning against spiritual compromise and the acceptance of what should be defeated.

sens: Sheep shearing place in the Northern Kingdom
H1044.detail: Beth-Éked is a place where sheep were gathered for shearing. The name literally means "house of the tying" or "house of shearing": it was a center for pastoral work. It was at this location that King Jehu met the princes of Judah (2 Kings 10:12-14).
H1044.origine: The Hebrew name is composed of two words: "beith" (house) and "eqed" (shearing or tying). It designates a building or area set up for sheep shearing operations, a common practice in the rural economy of the ancient Levant.
H1044.emploi: Beth-Éked appears only twice in the Bible, both in the account of Jehu's reign in 2 Kings 10. It was a recognizable and likely frequented place, as Jehu stationed there to meet the princes of Judah who were traveling. The mention of the location suggests its importance as a landmark in the territory of the Northern Kingdom.

sens: City in southern Judea
H1046.detail: Beth-Paleth is a small town mentioned in the southern mountainous region of Judea. It appears in the list of cities belonging to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:27), among the locations in the Negev and the southern region. Later, it is cited as one of the towns where the sons of Judah lived after the return from exile (Nehemiah 11:26). Its name literally means "house of escape" or "place of refuge," perhaps suggesting a place of safety in this southern region of Judea.
H1046.origine: The name Beth-Paleth is composed of two Hebrew words: "Beth" (בֵּית) means "house" or "dwelling," and "Paleth" (פָּלֶט) means "escape" or "refuge." The word "Paleth" is related to the Hebrew root of the verb "to escape" or "to flee." The full name thus evokes a house or place intended to serve as a refuge in the face of danger.
H1046.emploi: Beth-Paleth is mentioned exactly twice in the Scriptures. First in Joshua 15:27, in the enumeration of the cities assigned to the tribe of Judah, particularly those in the Negev (the southern desert). It reappears in Nehemiah 11:26, where it is listed among the cities where the sons of Judah settled after their return from the Babylonian exile. These two occurrences show that Beth-Paleth was a significant locality in southern Judea, important enough to be mentioned during the land distribution and repopulation of the country after the exile.

sens: Location in Transjordan, east of the Jordan
Valley where Israel camped before entering Canaan
Burial place of Moses
H1047.detail:
1. Beth-Peor is a city located east of the Jordan, in the region of the Amorites. The name literally means "house of Peor" — Peor likely being a local deity or a geographical feature. It was a mountainous region, with hills and heights (Joshua 13:20).

2. During the last stage of the journey in the desert, before entering Canaan, the Israelites camp in the valley opposite Beth-Peor (Deuteronomy 3:29). It is from this place that Moses addresses the people, reminding them of the laws and covenants of the Lord — hence the context of the entire book of Deuteronomy.

3. It is also the place where Moses was buried after his death. The Lord buried him "in the valley, in the land of Moab, opposite Beth-Peor," and no one knows his grave to this day (Deuteronomy 34:6). This detail emphasizes the unique and mysterious nature of the death of Israel's leader.
H1047.origine: The Hebrew name בֵּית פְּעוֹר (bet pe.or) literally means "house of Peor." Peor is the name of a mountain or region, possibly related to a local cult. This locality does not have a clear etymology in Hebrew, but it was well-known in the geography of the time of the Israelites.
H1047.emploi: Beth-Peor appears four times in the Bible, exclusively in Deuteronomy and Joshua. It is first mentioned as the valley where Israel stops before entering Canaan (Deuteronomy 3:29 and 4:46), then as the location of Moses' grave (Deuteronomy 34:6). Finally, it is listed among the cities assigned to the tribe of Reuben during the division of the territory (Joshua 13:20). All these references place Beth-Peor east of the Jordan, in the region conquered from Sihon, king of the Amorites.
H1047.portee: Beth-Peor marks a pivotal moment in Israel's history: it is the threshold of the Promised Land, where Moses imparts his final teachings before dying. The fact that Moses is buried in this place, rather than in Egypt or Canaan, underscores that God's promise extends beyond earthly life.

sens: City in the territory of Issachar in the Promised Land
H1048.detail: Beth-Patsets is a locality in the tribal territory of Issachar, listed among the cities assigned to this tribe during the division of the Promised Land. It appears in the list of cities of Issachar alongside Remeth, En-Gannim, and En-Hadda (Joshua 19:21).
H1048.origine: The Hebrew name literally means "house of the dispersion": בֵּית (bet, "house") combined with פַּצֵּץ (patstsés, "to scatter, disperse"). The etymology may reflect the geography of the place or an ancient characteristic of the region, although the exact meaning of this name for this locality is not clarified by biblical sources.
H1048.emploi: Beth-Patsets appears only once in the Bible, during the recounting of the territorial inheritance of Issachar in Joshua 19. It is mentioned in an administrative enumeration of the cities and villages assigned to this tribe during the conquest and division of Canaan under Joshua's leadership.

sens: Fortified city of Judea, in Israel
Strategic stronghold of the kingdom of Judah
H1049.detail: 1. Beth-Tsur is a city in Judea mentioned in the list of cities in the territory of Judah (Joshua 15:58). Its name literally means "house of the rock," which evokes a place established on a rocky height, typical of the geography of Judea. 2. This city had military and administrative importance: it is cited among the fortresses that King Rehoboam built to defend his kingdom (2 Chronicles 11:7), and it remained an important territorial center at the time of Nehemiah, as an administrative district chief resided there (Nehemiah 3:16).
H1049.origine: The Hebrew name Beth-Tsur is composed of two words: beth ("house," "dwelling") and tsur ("rock"). The image is that of a house built on stone, symbolizing solidity. The name reflects the topography of the site, established on a rocky elevation in the mountainous region of Judea.
H1049.emploi: Beth-Tsur appears four times in the Hebrew Bible. It is first listed as a city in the territory of Judah (Joshua 15:58), then mentioned as a stronghold built by King Rehoboam to fortify his kingdom (2 Chronicles 11:7). A genealogist mentions it in connection with Maon (1 Chronicles 2:45). Finally, at the time of Nehemiah, it retains its status as an administrative center: a district chief supervises the repairs of the walls of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 3:16).

sens: City in northern Israel, in the territory of Dan
Border region between Israel and Syria
H1050.detail:
1. Beth-Rehob is a city located in northern Israel, in the territory assigned to the tribe of Dan. The name literally means "house of the street" or "house of the public square." In Judges 18:28, it is mentioned as a geographical landmark marking the northern boundary of the valley where the Danites settled after their migration: the city was far from Sidon and isolated, which corresponded to the Danites' plans to settle freely.
2. Beth-Rehob also appears as an important Syrian city, likely the same locality that marked the border between Israel and the northern Aramean kingdoms. In 2 Samuel 10:6, it is listed among the strongholds where the Syrians recruited mercenaries to fight David: it was therefore a strategic region controlled by the Arameans, on the road to Hamath.
H1050.origine: The name Beth-Rehob means "house of the street" or "house of the square" in Hebrew: בֵּית (beït, house) and רְחוֹב (rechovv, street, public square). It is a toponym describing the nature or situation of the locality. The same root רְחוֹב (rechovv) simply gives "Rehob," which is a shorter variant of the same place name.
H1050.emploi: Beth-Rehob is mentioned twice in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in Judges and Samuel, and always as a major geographical landmark in the north. In Judges 18:28, it serves as a reference point for locating the valley where the Danites settled after fleeing the coastal region: the Bible emphasizes that the city was isolated and without alliances, making it an ideal refuge. In 2 Samuel 10:6, it is an Aramean power center from which Syrian troops departed; the Bible mentions it alongside other cities like Zobah and Maacah, showing that it was one of the military capitals of the region. In both cases, Beth-Rehob embodies the northern border between the Israelite world and the Aramean world.

sens: Man from the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H1051.detail: 1. Rapha is a man from the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:12. He is the son of Eshton and the brother of Paseach and Thechinna. The text presents him as the one who "begot the house of Rapha," which means he founded or named a family group or a place.
H1051.origine: The name Rapha literally means "house of healing" in Hebrew ("bêt" = house, "rapa" = to heal). It is a common theophoric or descriptive name in the Old Testament, where names reflect qualities, hopes, or circumstances of birth. This patronymic suggests an association with healing or restoration.
H1051.emploi: Rapha appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:12. He is listed in the genealogy of Judah, among a list of families and their descendants. The text places him in the context of the "men of Reca" and mentions that he had sons who founded or controlled cities. His role seems to be that of a clan ancestor whose name has been perpetuated in a family branch of Judah.

sens: Fortified city of Canaan, in Upper Galilee, in the tribe of Manasseh
H1052.detail: Beth-Shean is an important city in the Canaanite territory, located west of the Jordan in the region of Manasseh. It was among the cities that the Israelites were to conquer during their settlement in the Promised Land, but Manasseh failed to drive out its Canaanite inhabitants (Judges 1:27). It is notably the place where the Philistines displayed the corpse of King Saul and those of his sons after their victory at Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:10, 12), a humiliating event for Israel that the men of Jabesh rectified by secretly removing the bodies to honor them.
H1052.origine: The name literally means "house of." Beth-Shean or Beth-Shan (graphical variant) likely refers to an ancient Canaanite settlement site. It was a strategic city along the Jezreel Valley, an important crossroads in antiquity.
H1052.emploi: Beth-Shean appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the books of Joshua, Judges, and Samuel. It is first mentioned as a border city of the territory that Manasseh was to occupy, but the Canaanites firmly maintained their hold there, possessing iron chariots (Joshua 17:11, 16; Judges 1:27). Its military importance is confirmed by the dramatic episode of 1 Samuel 31, where it becomes the scene of Saul's posthumous humiliation. It is also listed among the administrative districts of Solomon's kingdom (1 Kings 4:12).

sens: City in the southwest of Judah, in the Sorek Valley
Transit point between the territory of Israel and that of Judah
Site of a significant event: the arrival of the Ark of the Covenant in Israelite territory
H1053G.detail:
1. Beth-Shemesh is a city located in the southwest of the territory of Judah, near the fertile Sorek Valley. Its name, which means "house of the sun" in Hebrew, may reflect the religious or geographical significance of the place. It is mentioned as a territorial boundary in Joshua 15:10, appearing in the borders of Judah.

2. The city served as a transit point between different territories. It is mentioned as an administrative stop in 1 Kings 4:9, where it is listed among the districts that King Solomon established for the supply of the kingdom, demonstrating its strategic and economic importance.

3. Beth-Shemesh is best known as the place where the Ark of the Covenant, captured by the Philistines, was miraculously returned to Israel. According to 1 Samuel 6:13-19, the inhabitants, who were harvesting in the valley, saw the Ark and rejoiced, but the Lord struck down those who looked inside the Ark, revealing God's absolute holiness.
H1053G.origine: The Hebrew name בֵּית שֶׁמֶשׁ (beit shemesh) is composed of two words: "beit" means "house" and "shemesh" means "sun." This combination literally describes a "house of the sun" or a "temple of the sun." The choice of this name reflects either a pre-Islamic solar cult or simply the exposure or significance of the site. It is a descriptive place name, common in biblical geography, that combines two simple elements to designate a specific locality.
H1053G.emploi: Beth-Shemesh appears about 15 times in the Old Testament. It is first mentioned as a territorial boundary of Judah (Joshua 15:10) and as a Levitical city (Joshua 21:16), assigned to the descendants of Aaron. Its most dramatic moment occurs during the return of the Ark of the Covenant from the land of the Philistines (1 Samuel 6). The inhabitants see the Ark miraculously arrive by means of cows, and although they rejoice at first, God strikes those who do not respect the holiness of the Ark. Later, the city becomes a site of conflict: it is the scene of a battle between the king of Israel Joash and the king of Judah Amaziah (2 Kings 14:13 and 2 Chronicles 25:21), where Joash captures Amaziah.

sens: City in the territory of Issachar in the land of Canaan
H1053H.detail: Beth-Shemesh is a city that belonged to the tribe of Issachar in northern Palestine. Its Hebrew name means "house of the sun" (beth = house, shemesh = sun), likely due to a sanctuary dedicated to the sun or a geographical feature. It was located near Tabor and led to the Jordan (Joshua 19:22).
H1053H.origine: The name is composed of two Hebrew words: "beth" (house) and "shemesh" (sun). Several cities bore this name in Israel, likely designating places of worship or remarkable sites related to the sun. The name reflects the importance of the sun in the geography and religion of the ancient Near East.
H1053H.emploi: Beth-Shemesh is mentioned only once in the Segond as one of the sixteen cities assigned to the tribe of Issachar during the division of Canaan (Joshua 19:22). It appears in the list of boundaries and localities of the territory of Issachar, serving as a geographical landmark.

sens: City of the tribe of Naphtali in the Promised Land
H1053I.detail: 1. Beth-Shemesh is a city assigned to the tribe of Naphtali during the division of the Promised Land. Its name literally means "house of the sun" or "temple of the sun" in Hebrew, possibly reflecting an earlier solar cult prior to Israelite occupation. It appears in the list of cities of Naphtali in Joshua 19:38, listed among nineteen localities assigned to this tribe.
H1053I.origine: The Hebrew name בֵּית שֶׁמֶשׁ (Beth-Shemesh) combines בֵּית (beth) which means "house" and שֶׁמֶשׁ (shemesh) which means "sun." This composition reveals the religious history of the place: it likely originally designated a sanctuary or high place dedicated to the worship of the sun before being incorporated into the territory of Israel. The same name appears elsewhere in Canaan, indicating that solar worship was a regional phenomenon in antiquity.
H1053I.emploi: Beth-Shemesh is mentioned twice in the Bible: in Joshua 19:38, it is named in the official enumeration of the nineteen cities assigned to the tribe of Naphtali after the conquest. In Judges 1:33, the text specifies that, contrary to the order of total conquest, the Naphtalites did not expel the Canaanite inhabitants of Beth-Shemesh (nor of Beth-Anath), but rather subjected them to tribute. This mention shows that some cities in Canaan were not completely conquered during the initial settlement of Israel, a recurring reality in the book of Judges.
H1053I.portee: Beth-Shemesh reminds the reader that the conquest of the Promised Land was neither instantaneous nor total: the Israelites often cohabited with the Canaanite peoples, dominating rather than eliminating them, which posed lasting spiritual challenges. This passage invites reflection on incomplete obedience and its consequences in the history of God's people.

sens: City of Egypt
Temple or sanctuary of the sun
H1053J.detail: 1. Beth-Shemesh is a city in Egypt, known in antiquity as Heliopolis. The prophet Jeremiah mentions it at the time when Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, conquers Egypt: the prophet announces that the king will break the statues found there (Jeremiah 43:13). It is a real place, significant in Egyptian religious history. 2. The name Beth-Shemesh literally means "house of the sun": it refers to a temple or sanctuary dedicated to the worship of the sun, which shows the religious importance of the site in ancient Egypt. The gods worshiped there were the idols of the Egyptians, which Jeremiah sees as objects destined for destruction.
H1053J.origine: The name is composed of two Hebrew words: "beit" (בֵּית) means "house" or "temple," and "shemesh" (שֶׁ֫מֶשׁ) means "sun." Beth-Shemesh is the Hebrew equivalent of the Greek name Heliopolis ("city of the sun"), which was the major center of worship for the Egyptian sun god Ra. The word "Shemesh" or "Schémesch" appears elsewhere in the Bible to refer to the sun itself.
H1053J.emploi: Beth-Shemesh appears only once in the Bible: in Jeremiah 43:13. The prophet Jeremiah mentions it in the context of Nebuchadnezzar's conquest of Egypt, the king of Babylon. Jeremiah prophesies that the Babylonian king will "break the statues of Beth-Shemesh" and "burn with fire the houses of the gods of Egypt." This is a pivotal moment where the Lord announces through His prophet the end of Egyptian paganism and the victory of the God of Israel over foreign idols.
H1053J.portee: The mention of Beth-Shemesh reminds the reader that the God of Israel also judges foreign nations and their idols. Even the prestigious and ancient temples of Egyptian powers cannot withstand the will of God. This affirms the sovereignty of the Lord over universal history and comforts Israel in exile: God controls the course of events, even when pagan empires seem to triumph.

sens: City of Judah
H1054.detail: Beth-Tappuah is a city of the tribe of Judah, mentioned in the list of Judean localities. Its name literally means "house of the apple" or "place of apples," suggesting that this region was known for fruit cultivation, probably apples or similar fruits. It is a small locality known only from this brief biblical passage.
H1054.origine: The name Beth-Tappuah is composed of two Hebrew words: "beth" (בית), which means "house" or "dwelling," and "tappuah" (תפּוח), which refers to the apple or a fruit from that tree. This type of geographical name was common in Israel, formed on the model "house of" + name of a product or characteristic of the place.
H1054.emploi: Beth-Tappuah appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:53, where it is listed among the cities allocated to the tribe of Judah during the division of the territory after the conquest. This mention is found in a long administrative list of Judean localities, indicating that it was an established and recognized city, even though it plays no major role in the biblical narrative.

sens: Royal residence, home of the king and his court
Building or part of a building where official receptions and feasts are held
Space or garden attached to the royal residence
H1055.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the royal house or palace, the dwelling where the king and his family live. In Esther 1:5, it refers to the "royal house" of Susa, the seat of power of the king of Persia, where the official festivities of the kingdom take place.
2. More specifically, it is the place where the king receives and holds his feasts: in Esther 7:7 and 7:8, the "garden of the palace" is the place where the king withdraws to reflect or calm down, distinct from the "banquet hall" where one eats and drinks. The palace thus includes gardens, courtyards, and reception halls.
3. The word can refer to both the building and the entire royal domain with its dependencies, meaning everything that belongs to the king's house and symbolizes his power and authority.
H1055.origine: The Hebrew word בִּיתָן (bitan) is formed from the root בַּיִת (bayit), which means "house." It literally means "house," but in a royal or noble context, it takes on the meaning of "palace," that is, a house of prestige and power. The suffix -ān or the particular vowels may express an amplified or specialized form of the simple word.
H1055.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Bible, all in the book of Esther, in chapters 1 and 7. It always refers to the royal residence of Susa, the capital of the Persian empire under King Ahasuerus. In Esther 1:5, it is the setting for the grand royal feast that lasts seven days. In Esther 7:7 and 7:8, the "garden of the palace" is the place where the king withdraws in his anger, contrasted with the "banquet hall" — which shows that the palace encompasses several distinct spaces, both interior and exterior. The word remains technical and specialized: it applies only to a royal residence, not to an ordinary house.
H1055.portee: This word reminds the reader of the importance of the royal setting in the story of Esther: it is in this palace, with its gardens and prestigious halls, that the intrigues unfold that lead to the salvation of the Jewish people. The palace is not just decoration: it is the symbol of the king's power and the place where destinies are decided, showing how God acts even in the heart of the most distant royal courts.

sens: valley of Palestine
place of weeping
H1056.detail: 1. Baca is a valley located in Palestine, mentioned only once in the Bible. Its name itself means "weeping" or "tears" in Hebrew, making it a place laden with sadness. 2. Although the psalmist speaks of this valley, he does not make it a place of despair: rather, in Psalms 84:7, the pilgrims who pass through it transform it into a source of blessing, as if the waters from heaven were watering the dry region and making it fertile. The meaning of the name (weeping) contrasts with the hope that the biblical text projects onto it.
H1056.origine: The Hebrew name בָּכָא (Baca) comes from a root that means "to weep," "to shed tears." What was a place marked by sorrow becomes, in the biblical perspective, a place where God transforms suffering into blessing. The geography of the name reflects a reality: it was probably a dry and difficult valley to traverse.
H1056.emploi: Baca appears only once in the Bible, in Psalms 84:7. The psalmist sings of the happiness of those who ascend to Jerusalem, the temple of God. By passing through the valley of Baca, these pilgrims do not encounter a barren desert, but a place where God pours out His blessings: "Who passing through the valley of Baca makes it a well; the rain also fills the pools." The context is that of a hymn of trust and joy in God's action for His children.
H1056.portee: For the believer reading this psalm, Baca teaches that the difficult valleys of life are not places abandoned by God. The very name (weeping) reminds us that suffering exists, but the psalm proclaims that God walks through it with us and transforms it into blessing. It is a promise: the path to God, even if it passes through trials, is accompanied by grace.

sens: Tree that produces balms and resins
Geographical location planted with these trees
H1057.detail: 1. The mulberry is an eastern tree that produces a valuable sap when it is cut — a resin or balm that is harvested for its virtues. David and his men are ordered to go around the Philistine army by passing through a place planted with these trees (2 Samuel 5:23). 2. This word also refers to the valley or grove where these trees grew, near Jerusalem. The sound of the wind in the tops of the mulberries becomes for David a divine sign that he should attack: "When you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the mulberry trees, then hurry, for the Lord will go out before you" (2 Samuel 5:24). This vivid detail shows how God concretely guides His servants through a landscape they know.
H1057.origine: The Hebrew word בָּכָא comes from a root that evokes the balm or resin that flows — the idea of something that flows or spreads. It is a well-known tree from the ancient Near East for its aromatic and medicinal properties. The biblical context — a grove visible from Jerusalem — suggests that it was a strategic and recognizable place in the Judean landscape.
H1057.emploi: This word appears only four times in the Hebrew Bible, all in parallel passages: 2 Samuel 5:23-24 and its doublet in 1 Chronicles 14:14-15. Both passages recount the same event — David's victory over the Philistines — and both mention the mulberries in the same strategic location. David must go around the enemy by passing near these trees, and the sound he hears there will be his signal to attack. It is a historical and geographical detail that anchors the narrative in a real landscape.
H1057.portee: This passage teaches that God guides His servants through concrete and natural signs — a sound in the trees becomes a divine word. David does not act according to his own calculations, but he listens to God even in the details of the terrain. This invites the believer to recognize God's presence and direction in the ordinary circumstances of life.

sens: To shed tears, to express emotion through weeping
To weep long or bitterly, often with groaning
To weep for someone, to express sorrow, mourning, or compassion for them
To weep before God, to express distress, repentance, or supplication in prayer
H1058.detail:
1. To weep is primarily to shed tears: it is a bodily reaction that manifests a deep emotion, joy or sorrow. Hagar weeps when she believes her child is condemned (Genesis 21:16), and Hezekiah sheds abundant tears while calling on the Lord (Isaiah 38:3).

2. To weep can also mean to weep bitterly, with force and persistence — the emotion becomes insistent and overwhelming. The Israelites weep bitterly when they long for the meat of Egypt (Numbers 11:4), and David weeps for a long time after the death of Absalom (2 Samuel 18:33).

3. To weep for someone means to weep in their presence or because of them, often to pay tribute or express mourning. King David weeps at the tomb of Abner (2 Samuel 3:32), and Jacob weeps for his son Joseph long after his disappearance (Genesis 37:35).

4. To weep before God means to express distress, repentance, or prayer in the divine presence, often while fasting. Nehemiah weeps, fasts, and prays when he learns of the ruin of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 1:4), and the Israelites weep before the Lord before going into battle (Judges 20:23).
H1058.origine: The Hebrew verb בָּכָה (bâkhâh) evokes the primary image of shedding tears. It belongs to a family of words from the ancient Near East related to the expression of emotions. Its root is very ancient and consistent in biblical Hebrew: it denotes a visible and audible act — one weeps, groans, emits sounds of sorrow. It is a verb in the Qal (simple voice) in most of its uses, but it can take marked forms (with the Piel) to intensify the idea of lamentation.
H1058.emploi: To weep is one of the most frequent verbs in the Hebrew Bible (about 100 occurrences), used in almost every book, from historical narratives to the Psalms. It is used to express mourning after a death (Jacob weeping for Joseph, David weeping for Abner or Absalom), supplication in distress (Nehemiah, Hannah, the Israelites in Egypt), regret or nostalgia (the Israelites weeping for the onions of Egypt), and even sometimes joy or joyful emotion (as in reunions). The context modifies the nuance: to weep can be a sign of mourning, revolt, repentance, or pleading prayer. In the Psalms, to weep becomes the expression of the cry of the righteous to God.
H1058.portee: The Bible does not hide tears: it shows them as a just and natural human reaction to loss, pain, or injustice. To weep before God is not a weakness, but a form of honest prayer that expresses trust in His compassion. For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that God sees our tears and that the Bible allows for true emotion, without guilt. Jesus Himself wept over Jerusalem and over Lazarus: to weep is a human reaction that God honors.

sens: Drop of water that flows from the eye
Weeping, physical manifestation of sadness or emotion
H1059.detail:
1. A tear is literally a drop of water that flows from the eye. It is the visible sign of weeping, what happens when one sheds tears.
2. The word also refers to the act of weeping itself, the emotion that causes these tears. In Ezra 10:1, the people of Israel "shed abundant tears": this is a true collective weeping, an outward manifestation of a deep emotion — here, repentance and pain over confessed unfaithfulness.
H1059.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to weep," "to shed tears." It denotes the natural and visible result of weeping: the drops that flow from the eyes. It is a simple and concrete word, related to the physical expression of feelings.
H1059.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezra 10:1. It is a solemn moment: Ezra, the scribe and priest, prays and confesses the sins of the people, and around him gathers a multitude — men, women, children — who shed abundant tears. This context shows that the tears here are the bodily expression of sincere and collective repentance for unfaithfulness to the covenant.
H1059.portee: Tears remind us that repentance is not just an intellectual or verbal act: it engages the whole being, including the body. Seeing the entire people weep together, including the children, shows the importance of publicly acknowledging our faults and sincerely lamenting them before God. It is a lesson on the authenticity of repentance.

sens: The first son or daughter born in a family
The young animal born first in a litter or generation
One who occupies the first place, rank, or primary inheritance in a group
One who has the rights and privileges of the elder
H1060.detail: 1. The firstborn is the child who is born first in a family: it is the eldest of the siblings. In Genesis 4:4, Abel offers "the firstborn of his flock," referring to the young animals that are born first. 2. In herds and lands, the firstborn holds particular religious and legal significance. In Exodus 13:2, the firstborn male, whether human or animal, is consecrated to God, and in Deuteronomy 14:23, the firstborn of the livestock is consumed before the Lord as an act of worship. 3. The firstborn inherits a position of power and responsibility: he receives a double portion of the paternal inheritance, as noted in the right of the firstborn in Deuteronomy 21:17. 4. The term is also used figuratively to denote one who holds the first place or represents a people. In Exodus 4:22, Israel is called "my son, my firstborn" to express that Israel occupies a privileged position among the nations.
H1060.origine: The Hebrew word בְּכוֹר comes from an ancient root meaning "to be strong, vigorous," associated with the role of leader or first. In biblical Hebrew, the firstborn carries the idea of priority, strength, and birthright. This word always designates one who is born or placed first, and it carries with it all the weight of custom and family responsibility among the ancient Hebrews.
H1060.emploi: The word appears about one hundred times in the Bible, especially in Genesis, Exodus, and Numbers, where it describes children ("Reuben, the firstborn" in Genesis 49:3), animals (the young animals offered in sacrifice), and legal family relationships. Exodus and Numbers make the consecration of the firstborn a ritual law: every male firstborn belongs to God, whether human or beast (Exodus 13:2, Numbers 3:40). In civil law, the firstborn receives a superior inheritance and may fulfill a role as head of the family (Deuteronomy 21:15-17). Figuratively, Israel is the "firstborn" of God, expressing its dignity and special covenant (Exodus 4:22). The term can also simply refer to the order of birth in a genealogy.
H1060.portee: For the believer, the firstborn reminds us that God chooses and consecrates: what is born first belongs to God, set apart for Him. This concept paves the way for the notion of Christ as the "firstborn," the one who has preeminence. It also teaches that position does not come from merit, but from God's design, and that it carries with it a responsibility towards God and others.

sens: The first harvests of the crop, those that ripen first
The sheaf or bread offered to God at the time of the Feast of Pentecost
What rightfully belongs to God as the first fruit of labor and the land
Figuratively: that which opens a series, that which comes in the vanguard
H1061.detail:
1. The firstfruits refer to the first fruits and grains that mature during seasonal harvests. It is the beginning of the harvest, before the general harvest. In Exodus 23:16 and 34:22, God commands a solemn feast of firstfruits, celebrated at Pentecost.
2. These first harvests were not to remain with the farmer: they were transformed into bread (Leviticus 23:20 mentions "the bread of the firstfruits") or presented as ground grain (Leviticus 2:14) and ritually offered to the Lord during a sacred feast. This act acknowledges that the land and its fruits belong to God.
3. The firstfruits then remain the portion of the priesthood or the poor. In Numbers 18:13, God promises the priest the firstfruits brought by the people. It is a due, not an optional gift.
4. The word evokes the idea of precedence and consecration: the first portions symbolize that all that follows also belongs to God, and that returning the firstfruits is to honor His sovereignty over life and work.
H1061.origine: The Hebrew word bikkurim comes from the root בכר (bakar), which means "to be or come before, to be first." It expresses the idea of priority in time. The firstfruits are literally "what comes first" in the agricultural cycle. This notion of "first" is found in other biblical words of the same family, but bikkurim is specialized in the realm of harvests and worship. It is a term loaded with religious significance: the first is never trivial in Israel; it belongs to God.
H1061.emploi: The word bikkurim appears about 15 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the law books (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers) that describe the ritual. The three major synodals of Israelite worship (Exodus 23:16 and 34:22, Leviticus 23) make it a central obligation: at Pentecost, the first harvests must be brought to the sanctuary. The remaining uses (2 Kings 4:42, Nehemiah, Ezekiel, Nahum) recall this practice or associate it with other offerings. The central idea remains stable: the firstfruits are what the people must offer to God without delay, in recognition of His blessing.
H1061.portee: For the believer, the firstfruits teach an essential spiritual truth: to recognize that everything comes from God and that offering Him the best of what we receive is not a loss, but an act of faith and worship. It is also an act of social justice, as the firstfruits benefited the priest and the poor. Offering to God what we have best first is to invert the natural order of selfishness and place the Lord at the heart of our economic and family life.

sens: The rights and privileges attached to the condition of being the firstborn son in a family
The inheritance or preferential share that the firstborn son receives
The position of first in the order of family succession
H1062.detail:
1. The birthright is the special right recognized for the firstborn son: he inherits a larger share than his brothers (often double) and occupies a place of honor in the family. This is what Esau naturally possessed as the firstborn son of Isaac until he sold it to Jacob for a bowl of lentils (Genesis 25:31-34).

2. This right also confers moral and religious authority: the firstborn is recognized as head of the family and heir of the promises made to the ancestors. When Esau reproaches Jacob for having taken this right, he understands that he has lost much more than just a share of material inheritance — he has lost his status and future (Genesis 27:36).

3. At the table, this birthright is also manifested in the order of precedence: Joseph's brothers sit according to their rank, the firstborn in the place of honor (Genesis 43:33). It is a visible sign of the status conferred by birth.
H1062.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root "bkr" (בכר) which means "to be the firstborn." It is formed with the suffix "-ah" (ה) which creates an abstract noun. The word literally designates "what belongs to the firstborn." This same root is found in "bekhor" (בְּכוֹר), which simply means "firstborn": the birthright is thus the quality or right of the bekhor.
H1062.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost entirely in the story of Jacob and Esau (6 occurrences in Genesis 25-27). It designates the legal and cultural right of the firstborn. In this story, Esau sells his birthright to Jacob for a meal — an extraordinary act that shows his contempt for this spiritual and material heritage. The word reappears in Genesis 43:33 to show how Joseph respects this order of birth at the table, and in the laws of Deuteronomy 21:17 which guarantee the firstborn son the right to a double portion of inheritance. The use in Chronicles highlights the lasting consequences: Reuben, the firstborn son of Jacob, loses his birthright because of his sin.
H1062.portee: This notion reveals the importance that biblical culture places on family order and each person's responsibility towards their heritage — both material and spiritual. The story of Esau warns the reader: it is possible to despise, through carelessness or impatience, what rightfully belongs to us and what calls us to greater responsibility. It also invites us to recognize that in God's plan, the natural order of things can be surprising: it is the younger Jacob, not the elder Esau, who receives the promised blessing.

sens: Fig that ripens first on the tree, before the general harvest
By extension: early fruit, first fruits
Sign of divine favor or blessing
Conversely: sign of weakness or vulnerability when it is left defenseless
H1063.detail: 1. The early fig is one that ripens ahead of the season, as soon as the first fruits appear on the fig tree. Isaiah describes it: tiny and solitary, barely in the hand before it is swallowed, it symbolizes something fragile and ephemeral (Isaiah 28:4). 2. The term more broadly refers to the first fruits of the harvest — what comes before the others. Jeremiah speaks of the "figs of the first harvest" as a distinct, superior category: these figs are excellent, visibly chosen (Jeremiah 24:2). 3. In God's mouth, this image evokes blessing and election: He found Israel as "the first fruits of a fig tree," meaning rare, promising, predestined to be good (Hosea 9:10). 4. But the same word also paints distress: the prophet Micah feels like someone searching for early fruits of the harvest and finds none — an emptiness, a disappointment (Micah 7:1).
H1063.origine: The Hebrew word bikkurah (בִּכּוּרָה) comes from the root bik (ב-כ), related to beginning, first, what comes forward. The same root produces "firstborn" (bekhor) and "first fruits" (bikkurim). The image is that of the first fruit that emerges, that shows itself before the others — a very concrete, agricultural notion observed in Mediterranean orchards where a few figs ripen alone before the harvest.
H1063.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, always in the singular or in the context of first fruits. Isaiah uses it for the fragility of an isolated fig that is quickly swallowed. Jeremiah uses it to distinguish first-quality figs. Hosea presents it as an image of Israel's primitive goodness. Micah invokes it to express a vain quest. The word thus oscillates between two poles: on one side, the excellence and rarity of the first fruit; on the other, its vulnerability and the uncertainty of its persistence.
H1063.portee: This early fig reminds us that God chooses what is first, excellent, destined — Israel was His "first fruits" before the fall. It also invites us to seek signs of favor and divine presence in beginnings: the first fruits of the Spirit, the first fruits of the resurrection. But it warns us: what is beautiful and early can also escape us quickly if we neglect or reject it.

sens: Benjaminite ancestor of King Saul
H1064.detail: Becorath is a man from the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Samuel 9:1, in the genealogy of King Saul. He is the son of Aphiach and the father of Zeror, making him an important link in the genealogical chain leading back to Saul, the first king of Israel.
H1064.origine: The name Becorath literally means "firstborn" (from the Hebrew root that designates the right of primogeniture). It is a Benjaminite family name that perhaps underscores the genealogical importance of this lineage within the tribe.
H1064.emploi: Becorath appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 9:1, where he is listed in the complete genealogy of Saul. This man has no active role recounted in the Old Testament: he is mentioned only as an ancestor of the king, which shows that ancient scribes valued preserving the royal lineage from its roots in the tribe of Benjamin.

sens: The action of shedding tears
The flowing of a liquid
Collective lamentation, pain expressed in tears
Grief, penitence through tears
H1065.detail:
1. To weep denotes the action of shedding tears, often a gesture of intense emotion. When Joseph reveals his identity to his brothers, he "raises his voice, weeping" (Genesis 45:2): the tears mark an overflow of feeling, joy or sorrow. Hezekiah also "spills abundant tears" while praying to the Lord (2 Kings 20:3), showing how supplication engages the whole heart.
2. The word can also refer to the flowing of water or a liquid: in Job 28:11, it speaks of the "flowing of waters" that God stops by digging mines. It is the same verb, applied to what flows like tears.
3. To weep also evokes lamentation, the collective expression of pain. Moab weeps for its ruined cities (Isaiah 15:2), Jeremiah wants to weep and moan over the burned mountains (Jeremiah 9:10): tears become the language of those who behold desolation.
4. Tears mark penitence and mourning. When the community hears of impending doom, they fast, weep, and don sackcloth (Isaiah 22:12, Joel 2:12): to weep is to acknowledge oneself as a sinner or in mourning, an act of repentance before God.
H1065.origine: The Hebrew word בְּכִי comes from the root בכה, "to weep." This root expresses the cry and gesture of tears, a vivid image of overflowing emotion. It appears in many biblical contexts: weeping for joy, sorrow, or repentance. The noun "weeping" (בְּכִי) names the act or state of one who sheds tears.
H1065.emploi: The word "to weep" (בְּכִי) appears 29 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah) and lamentation texts. In historical narratives (Genesis, 2 Samuel, 2 Kings), it marks a crucial emotional moment: Joseph weeps upon revealing himself, Hezekiah while imploring God. The prophets use it to describe weeping over destroyed cities or the unfaithful people: Jeremiah wants to weep "over the mountains" (Jeremiah 9:10). In the Psalms, tears are offered to God in prayer (Psalms 6:9, 102:10). The word designates both intimate emotion and the public act of mourning or penitence.
H1065.portee: Weeping in the Bible is never shameful: it is entrusting one's heart to God, confessing weakness, repentance, or love. Seeing the righteous and the prophets shed tears (Joseph, Hezekiah, Jeremiah) teaches us that the sincerity of the heart is also expressed through tears. God does not ignore our tears; He sees them and responds. It is a reminder that our faith is not primarily a matter of reason, but of a heart encounter with the Lord.

sens: Place near Gilgal where the Israelites wept
H1066.detail: Bokim is a place located near Gilgal (or near Bethel according to some interpretations), where the children of Israel shed tears. The name means "weeping" or "one who weeps," and it recalls a solemn moment of regret and repentance of the people. In Judges 2:1-5, a messenger of the Lord reproaches the Israelites for transgressing the covenant by not driving out the inhabitants of the land; at these words, the whole people bursts into tears, and the place receives this name for that reason.
H1066.origine: The name Bokim comes from the Hebrew root בכה (baka), which means "to weep." It is a meaningful name given to the place because of the historical event that took place there: the weeping of the people in recognizing their disobedience. The same term is used in other biblical accounts to describe tears of pain, repentance, or mourning.
H1066.emploi: Bokim is mentioned twice in the book of Judges, in verses 1 and 5 of chapter 2. It is a theological place rather than a major city: it appears only in this passage where the angel of the Lord admonishes Israel for its unfaithfulness to the covenant. The people respond with sincere tears and offer sacrifices to the Lord. This place thus marks a spiritual turning point at the beginning of the period of the judges, when Israel becomes aware of its guilt.
H1066.portee: Bokim teaches us that true repentance is accompanied by sincere tears and acknowledgment of sin. It is also a reminder that God speaks with compassion even when He corrects His people, and that divine correction aims to bring the heart back to the covenant. The tears shed at Bokim are not an end in themselves, but the beginning of a restoration of the relationship with God.

sens: the firstborn daughter, the one who was born first
more broadly, the one who has the rank of firstborn in succession or inheritance
H1067.detail: 1. This word simply designates the daughter who is born first in a family. In Genesis 19:31, Lot's two daughters refer to themselves: the elder and the younger. It is a matter of birth order. 2. By extension, the word carries the idea of rank and the rights attached to it: the elder has a special status, particularly in matters of marriage and inheritance. Laban appeals to custom in Genesis 29:26 to justify giving the elder daughter in marriage before the younger.
H1067.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to be first" or "to be born first." It belongs to the same family as the more common word "bekhor," which designates the firstborn (without gender distinction). This feminine form "bekirah" is used exclusively for daughters, while the masculine form applies to sons and, in a figurative context, to creatures or things.
H1067.emploi: This word appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible, always referring to firstborn daughters. The main usages are in Genesis 19 (the daughters of Lot), where the term appears 4 times to clarify who is the elder in the drama of Sodom. It also appears in Genesis 29:26 to establish the custom of marriage (the elder before the younger) and in 1 Samuel 14:49 to name the two daughters of Saul, Merab the elder and Michal the younger. The context is always that of lineage and order of succession.
H1067.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of birth order in the biblical world. The position of elder, even for a daughter, conferred responsibilities and rights. In faith, this may invite the reader to reflect on how God honors different roles in a family and how the order established by Him deserves respect.

sens: period of weeping and mourning following a death
visible manifestation of grief through tears and cries
deep affliction in the face of loss
H1068.detail: 1. The word primarily designates the official mourning period, the time when one withdraws to grieve for the dead. In the passage from Genesis, Joseph waits for "the days of mourning" to pass before speaking to Pharaoh: it is a clearly defined phase, between death and the return to ordinary life (Genesis 50:4). 2. This time of mourning is not silent: it is filled with tears, cries, and visible signs of grief. Weeping is its natural and expected expression. 3. More broadly, the word evokes intimate affliction, the sincere sorrow of the heart in the face of the death of a loved one.
H1068.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the act of weeping, shedding tears. It describes not only the act of crying but also the state of the one who mourns — mourning as a period and as a condition of the soul. It is a simple and concrete term, rooted in the universal human experience of loss.
H1068.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Genesis 50:4, where it designates the time Joseph dedicates to weeping and funeral rites after the death of his father Jacob. The text shows that this mourning was a respected time, with a specific duration, before returning to ordinary affairs. It is a word that the biblical text borrows to express a social reality: the recognized necessity to mourn one's dead and not to return immediately to public life.
H1068.portee: Mourning is a reality that God acknowledges and respects. The Bible does not forbid tears in the face of death; it admits their legitimacy and even ordains them, giving the dead a time for weeping. This teaches that sadness has its place, that mourning those we loved is not a lack of faith, but a human and rightful expression of the heart.

sens: To be born first among the children of the same mother
To bear or give birth to a first child
To produce the first fruits, speaking of a tree or plant
To confer or recognize the status of firstborn
H1069.detail:
1. The primary meaning is factual: to be the first child born of a mother. It is a state of birth, a family reality. In Leviticus 27:26, the firstborn of the livestock belongs to the Lord by virtue of its condition.
2. The verb can also mean to bear or give birth to a child for the first time — the primordial act of childbirth. Jeremiah 4:31 speaks of "cries of anguish like in a first childbirth," referring to the pains of one who gives birth for the first time.
3. Figuratively, the verb applies to trees and fruits: to ripen, to produce its fruits. In Ezekiel 47:12, the trees "will bear fruit" every month, meaning they will regularly produce their fruits.
4. The verb can also express a legal or social act: to institute someone as firstborn, to recognize or confer this status. Deuteronomy 21:16 prohibits a father from "recognizing as firstborn" the son of his preferred wife if he is not actually the elder.
H1069.origine: The root בכר (b-k-r) evokes the idea of primacy and new youth. It also appears in the name בְכוֹר (bekhor, "firstborn"), which designates the one who is born first. In Hebrew, this family of words expresses both the biological fact (being born before others) and its religious and social importance (right of primogeniture, consecration to God).
H1069.emploi: The verb appears four times in the Hebrew Bible. It first designates the condition of the firstborn within the framework of the Law (Leviticus, Deuteronomy): the firstborn belongs to the Lord and enjoys special rights; one cannot arbitrarily "recognize" as firstborn a son who is not the elder. It is also used for the act of giving birth (Jeremiah): the "cries of the first childbirth" evoke the sufferings of the mother giving birth for the first time. Finally, the verb extends to the agricultural domain (Ezekiel): the trees of the restored paradise "will bear fruit" each month, an image of inexhaustible fertility.
H1069.portee: This word reminds us of the biblical importance of primogeniture: God claims the firstborn as a sign of covenant and consecration. But it also emphasizes that the natural order (who is born first) does not always determine the divine order (God can choose the younger). The word also speaks of renewed fertility and promise: the restored land will bear fruit forever.

sens: young camel with one hump
pack and saddle camel suited for deserts
animal of prestige and wealth
H1070.detail: 1. The dromedary is a young camel, specifically a camel with a single hump, distinct from the camel with two humps. It is this animal that is seen in the arid regions of the Middle East and North Africa. 2. The dromedary was a remarkably well-suited animal for transport and riding on long desert journeys: fast, enduring, capable of carrying heavy loads for days. 3. Owning dromedaries signified wealth and power: in Isaiah 60:6, the peoples come to Jerusalem "covered with a multitude of camels, dromedaries of Midian and Ephah," immense herds that testify to the prosperity and magnificence of those who lead them.
H1070.origine: The Hebrew word beker comes from a root evoking the idea of youth and vigor. It specifically designates the young camel or dromedary, an emblematic animal of the trade routes that crossed Arabia. The Hebrew term corresponds to similar words in neighboring Semitic languages, where it always retains this meaning of a robust and precious animal.
H1070.emploi: The word appears only once in the biblical text (Isaiah 60:6), in a grand prophetic vision where Jerusalem, restored and glorified, receives the riches of the nations. The dromedaries are among the treasures that distant peoples — particularly those from Midian, Ephah, and Sheba, prosperous regions of the south and east — bring as tribute and homage. Their presence underscores both the prosperity of the moment and the geographical extent of this future restoration.
H1070.portee: This passage invites contemplation of the promise of a restored Jerusalem, towards which the riches of the peoples will converge. The dromedaries symbolize not only material wealth but also the future unity of nations around God, reminding the Christian reader that the glory of God will one day draw all peoples to Him.

sens: son of Benjamin, head of a Benjaminite family
ancestor of a branch of the tribe of Benjamin
H1071G.detail: 1. Béker is a man from the tribe of Benjamin mentioned for the first time at the time of Israel's descent into Egypt (Genesis 46:21).
