He is one of the ten sons of Benjamin listed that day, alongside his brothers Bela, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, and others. 2. Béker becomes the founder of an important Benjaminite lineage. His nine sons — Zemira, Joash, Eliezer, Eljoenai, Omri, Jeremoth, Abijah, Anathoth, and Alameth — are listed in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 7, showing that his descendants prospered and formed a significant house within the tribe.
H1071G.origine: The name Béker means "young camel" in Hebrew, likely given because of its speed or strength. It is not a theophoric name (not containing the name of God), but rather a descriptive or animal name, which was common among the ancient Israelites.
H1071G.emploi: Béker appears three times in the Scriptures, always in genealogical lists. First mentioned in Genesis 46:21 among the descendants of Jacob who went down to Egypt, he is then cited in 1 Chronicles 7:6-8 as one of the three major sons of Benjamin (along with Bela and Jediael), and a detailed list of his nine sons is provided there. These appearances confirm his importance in the genealogical structure of the tribe of Benjamin, particularly his role as the founder of an influential branch. Although few personal details are given, his constant presence in the genealogies indicates that he was a key figure in his tribe.

sens: Son of Ephraim, head of a family during the wilderness period
H1071H.detail: 1. Béker is a son of Ephraim mentioned only once in the Bible, during the census of the Israelites in the wilderness (Numbers 26:35). He founds a family, that of the Bakrites, which bears his name. His brothers are Shutelach, Tahan, Ezer, Elead, and Beriah.
H1071H.origine: The name Béker literally means "young camel" in Hebrew. It is a descriptive name, like many biblical names. The descendants of Béker are called "Bakrites" (בַּכְרִי), according to the Hebrew practice of adding the suffix -ite or -ite to the names of ancestors to designate their descendants.
H1071H.emploi: Béker appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:35, in the context of the second census of the Israelites in the wilderness, after the exodus from Egypt. This passage lists the sons of Ephraim and the families they founded. Béker is included as one of the sons of Ephraim whose descendants are counted among the people of Israel.

sens: Young female domesticated animal, of the camelid family
H1072.detail: 1. The young camel is a young female domesticated animal. It is a robust and useful pack animal in the desert, capable of carrying loads and traveling long distances without water — much more than a horse or donkey. The Hebrew word מֵן (bikh.rah) specifically refers to this animal in its youth, distinguished from the adult camel.
H1072.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "first, eldest" or "new, young." The young camel is thus the animal in its youth, comparable to the sense of "first" or "firstborn." In Hebrew, animal names are often formed with suffixes or modifications that indicate age or gender; here the feminine and diminutive form emphasizes youth.
H1072.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 2:23. The prophet uses it to describe a wild camel wandering in the desert, who, in its agitation, does not know where it is going — an image of the lost people of Israel chasing after idols. This comparison highlights instability and wandering: while the young camel possesses an instinct that guides it, Israel has willingly lost its way by abandoning God.
H1072.portee: This image of the young camel reveals how Scripture speaks to the ears of the peoples of the Middle East: it draws from their experience of life in the desert to describe spiritual agitation and wandering. For the reader today, it reminds us that straying far from God is like a lost beast that has lost its way — a fruitless agitation. It is an invitation to return to the one who alone can guide us.

sens: Son of Azel, from the tribe of Benjamin during the divided monarchy
H1074.detail: 1. Bocru is a man from the tribe of Benjamin mentioned in the genealogies of the time of the divided monarchy. He was one of the six sons of Azel, alongside Azrikam, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan (1 Chronicles 8:38 and 9:44).
H1074.origine: The name Bocru comes from ancient Hebrew and literally means "firstborn" or "eldest." It is a descriptive name that likely characterized the birth order in Azel's family, although in the biblical text he is not explicitly presented as the eldest of the six sons.
H1074.emploi: Bocru appears only twice in the Bible, both in the Book of Chronicles: in chapters 8 and 9 of 1 Chronicles. He is listed in the genealogies of the tribe of Benjamin, where the descendants of important families are enumerated. These two mentions of the same verse (which appears twice in the text) testify to the importance given to the preservation of Israelite genealogies after the exile. Bocru has no personal story reported in the Bible; we only know of his existence by his name in these genealogical trees.

sens: A Benjamite man during the united monarchy of Israel
Father of Sheba, who revolts against King David
Leader of a revolt pursued by David's generals
H1075.detail: Bicri is a Benjamite mentioned in the second century of the monarchy of Israel. He is the father of Sheba, who proclaims a revolt against King David shortly after Absalom's rebellion: "Sheba, son of Bicri, a Benjamite" (2 Samuel 20:1) sounds the trumpet and calls the Israelites to abandon the king. Sheba, son of Bicri, becomes a fugitive on the run: David sends his generals Joab and Abishai to pursue him. This name appears in the accounts of the pursuit of Sheba, always to identify the father of the rebel (2 Samuel 20:2, 20:6, 20:7, 20:10, 20:13).
H1075.origine: The name Bicri, in Hebrew בִּכְרִי, means "youth" or "youthful." It belongs to the family of Benjamite patronymic names. His son Sheba is designated as "Bicrite" (בֵּרִים bikh.rim) by his patronymic, according to the Hebrew custom of identifying people by their father's name.
H1075.emploi: Bicri appears only in chapter 20 of 2 Samuel, in the account of Sheba's revolt against David. He is mentioned six times, always as the father of Sheba ("Sheba, son of Bicri"), never directly as an actor. Each mention reinforces the identity of the rebel and recalls his belonging to the tribe of Benjamin, a relevant political detail since Benjamin, the tribe of the first king Saul, had reasons to feel the predominance of Judah. The repetition of the patronymic creates a narrative continuity in the pursuit of the rebel.
H1075.portee: This passage teaches that revolts against legitimate authority, even among the people of God, meet justice. Sheba, son of Bicri, despite his attempt to split, is pursued and annihilated. For the Christian, this reminds us of the importance of order and submission to the authority established by God.

sens: descendant de Béker, fils d'Éphraïm
H1076.detail: 1. Bakrite designates a member of the family descended from Béker, son of Ephraim. Béker was one of the sons of Ephraim during the time of Egypt and the Exodus. The term is a gentilice (a word denoting family or tribal affiliation). In Numbers 26:35, after the exodus from Egypt, Moses conducts a census of the Israelites by families, and the Bakrites appear alongside the Shuthelahites and the Tachanites, all descendants of Ephraim. Like all biblical gentilices, this word expresses genealogical identity and family heritage within the tribe of Ephraim.
H1076.origine: Bakrite comes from the name Béker (which literally means 'firstborn' or 'eldest'), son of Ephraim mentioned in the genealogy of Israel. The common Hebrew suffix for forming a gentilice (belonging to a family or clan) transforms the father's name into the name of the clan of descendants. Béker himself is derived from a root meaning 'young camel' or 'eldest', but the proper name has established itself as the genealogical identifier of the family.
H1076.emploi: The word Bakrite appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:35. It is in the context of the census of the Israelites at the end of the desert, when God commands Moses to count the people by tribes and families before entering Canaan. The Bakrites are listed among the sons of Ephraim, with no particular detail about their importance or number. Like other tribal gentilices, this term falls under the administrative and genealogical register of the Bible, serving to identify the family groups that structure Israel.

sens: principal dieu babylonien
idole ou fausse divinité
H1078.detail:
1. Bel is the name of the supreme god of the Babylonian pantheon, honored particularly in Babylon. It is a powerful deity to whom the Babylonians attributed dominion and victory. Isaiah 46:1 mentions him alongside Nebo as an object of Babylonian worship.
2. For the biblical prophets, Bel represents a vain idol, a false god incapable of saving. Jeremiah 50:2 announces that 'Bel is confounded', meaning that this supposed divine power collapses and reveals itself powerless in the face of divine judgment. Jeremiah 51:44 reinforces this idea by declaring that God will punish Bel and stop the worship that flowed to him from the nations.
H1078.origine: Bel comes from Babylonian and means 'lord' or 'master'. It is the title given to the god Marduk, the principal deity of the Babylonian pantheon. The name may be related to Semitic roots denoting lordship, but here it is a direct borrowing from Babylonian worship as the Hebrews knew it during the exile or through contact with Babylon.
H1078.emploi: Bel appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, all in prophetic texts concerning Babylon. Isaiah 46:1 refers to him as a Babylonian idol carried by animals, symbolizing his weakness. Jeremiah 50:2 and 51:44 name him in oracles of judgment announcing the fall of Babylon and the end of the worship rendered to this deity. These three passages use Bel to embody the false gods of Babylon, destined to be broken and lose their influence.
H1078.portee: For the Christian reader, Bel embodies the illusion of human powers that rebel against the true God. These prophecies show that idols, even those of the most powerful empires, are vain and fall before God. They invite us not to fear the gods or systems of the world, but to place our trust in God alone, who alone is eternal and true.

sens: The central or vital part of something
What one ardently wishes for, what one deeply desires
Intelligence, the ability to understand and reflect
Feelings and emotions
Will and intentions
H1079.detail:
1. The heart is primarily the physical organ at the center of the body. But in the Bible, it signifies much more: the seat of a person's deepest thoughts, emotions, and decisions.
2. It is what we truly care about, what we intensely and sincerely desire. In Daniel 6:14, the king puts his whole heart into wanting to save Daniel: this is his true concern, the one that drives him to act.
3. It is also the place of intelligence and reason. To have heart is to be capable of understanding, reflecting, and judging.
4. The heart is the home of emotions: joy, sadness, fear, love. It is where our truest feelings are born.
5. Finally, the heart represents deep will, what truly drives us to act. It is the center of who we really are.
H1079.origine: This Aramaic word "bal" comes directly from the Hebrew root "lev" (לֵב), the fundamental biblical word for heart. It appears in many Hebrew expressions where the heart is the seat of all that is essential within us: our thoughts, desires, intentions. Aramaic takes up this same conception of the heart as the vital center of inner life.
H1079.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 6:14. It is an Aramaic text from the Book of Daniel, as this section (Daniel 2:4 to 7:28) is written in Aramaic, the language spoken in Mesopotamia during the exile. King Darius desperately seeks to save Daniel from the lions: he "takes to heart" his deliverance, meaning it becomes his major concern and he acts with all his energy to accomplish it. This usage shows the heart as the seat of will and personal commitment.
H1079.portee: This word reminds us that what we truly care about reveals who we are. King Darius, through his sincere desire to save Daniel, shows that his heart is sensitive to justice and friendship. For the Christian reader, it invites reflection: what do I truly care about? What does my deep heart desire and pursue? For it is there that our faithfulness to God and His values is played out.

sens: Gradually reduce through friction, wear
Fatigue, weaken someone through repeated actions
Harass, constantly persecute (figurative sense)
H1080.detail: 1. The verb primarily describes physical wear: something that wears down, gradually reducing through friction or time. 2. It also applies to a person who is tired or weakened by repeated efforts, as if being gradually exhausted. 3. In a figurative sense, it denotes constant harassment or persecution: in Daniel 7:25, the wicked king "will wear down the saints of the Most High" by oppressing them relentlessly, seeking to break them through repeated attacks on their faith, laws, and identity.
H1080.origine: The Aramaic root בְּלָא (bela) evokes the fundamental image of progressive wear, like an object that years or friction reduce. The derived sense of persecution or harassment arises from this image: to wear someone down is to torment them endlessly, to gradually reduce them.
H1080.emploi: This verb appears once in the Bible, in Daniel 7:25, a key passage of apocalyptic prophecy. It describes the action of the wicked king (the fourth beast) against the saints of God: he "wears them down" or "oppresses" them through constant persecution. The context shows that this harassment is both political ("will oppress") and religious ("will seek to change the times and the law"). The image of "wearing down" emphasizes the persistent and trying nature of this persecution.
H1080.portee: This word reminds us that persecution is not always sudden violence, but often slow and continuous harassment. For the Christian facing opposition, it invites recognition that repeated attacks on their faith, convictions, or religious identity are part of the trials that God allows. It also highlights the reality of the suffering of the saints throughout history, while reminding (through the prophetic context) that God remains sovereign and His victory is assured.

sens: father of Merodach-Baladan, king of Babylon
H1081.detail: Baladan is the father of Merodach-Baladan, a king of Babylon mentioned during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He never appears directly in the biblical narrative, but his name is cited as the genealogy of his son Merodach-Baladan, who sent an embassy to Hezekiah after his healing (2 Kings 20:12 and Isaiah 39:1).
H1081.origine: The name means "Bel is (his) lord," composed of the name of the Babylonian god Bel and a formula of belonging. It is a typical name from ancient Mesopotamia, revealing the religious beliefs of this pagan region.
H1081.emploi: Baladan appears only twice in the Bible, always to identify the father of Merodach-Baladan, king of Babylon, during the time of King Hezekiah of Judah. The two occurrences (2 Kings 20:12 and Isaiah 39:1) recount the same event: the sending of an embassy with a letter and gift to Hezekiah following his recovery from a serious illness.

sens: Let out a breath, catch one's breath
Find a moment of relaxation, relief
Express joy, show a smiling face
Burst forth, manifest suddenly
H1082.detail:
1. The primary sense is physical: to catch one's breath after effort or fatigue. Job asks God, "Let Him withdraw from me, and let me breathe a little" (Job 10:20) — he is simply seeking a respite, a moment where he can breathe without the crushing pressure of suffering.
2. To breathe also means to find moral relief, to regain lightness after distress. Job 9:27 contrasts the desire to "breathe" and "regain courage" with the crushing of his sufferings.
3. The word can express joy or cheerfulness: a face that breathes, that lights up, that shows joy — the idea of smiling or inner clarity.
4. In a rarer image, to breathe can mean "to burst forth" or "to manifest" suddenly, like a ruin that suddenly appears: "He brings ruin upon the mighty" (Amos 5:9).
H1082.origine: The Hebrew word expresses the idea of breath and lightness. It comes from a root that paints the image of free breathing, of relaxation of body and spirit. The underlying image is that of relief after tension, of relief that allows one to breathe freely again — which is why the word naturally glides from the physical (catching one's breath) to the moral (feeling better, being relieved or joyful).
H1082.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in contexts of suffering and distress. Job uses it twice to express his desire to escape the pressure of his torments and to breathe a little, if only briefly to feel relief (Job 9:27 and 10:20). Psalm 39:14 uses it in the same register, the psalmist pleading with God to turn His gaze away so that he can finally breathe before dying. Amos 5:9 uses the word in a radically different context, speaking of the ruin that "bursts forth" or "breaks out" upon the mighty — here the word evokes the idea of a sudden and striking manifestation. Through these usages, the word expresses either the relief sought by the suffering one or a sudden and powerful manifestation.
H1082.portee: For the believing reader, this word reminds us that even in the most intense suffering, there is a desire to escape, to breathe, to find a moment of peace. It also shows that the cry of the unfortunate to God is legitimate — Job dares to ask for respite. At the same time, it invites us to remember that our breathing, our relief, depends solely on God: it is to Him that we address this request. The word also speaks to us of regained freedom, of burdens lifted, images that speak of grace.

sens: Priest of the fifteenth class during the time of David
H1083G.detail: Bilga is a priest mentioned only once in the Bible, in the context of the classification of priests into twenty-four courses or groups of service. During the time of King David, the organization of worship at the temple required that the priests take turns regularly. Bilga led the fifteenth of these twenty-four teams of service (1 Chronicles 24:14).
H1083G.origine: The name Bilga means "joy" or "glee" in Hebrew, derived from a root expressing cheerfulness. Its unique occurrence in 1 Chronicles 24 suggests that this name was preserved in the memory of the people as that of a notable leader of a priestly class during the time of David.
H1083G.emploi: Bilga appears only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 24:14, where he is named among the leaders of the twenty-four courses of priests established by David. This administrative document from the first book of Chronicles preserves the names of all the leaders of the priestly divisions, and Bilga holds the rank of fifteenth.
H1083G.portee: This name reminds us that the service of God was organized with order and regularity, and that each servant had an assigned place in communal worship. It also illustrates how God took care to structure the priestly ministry so that the temple could function without interruption.

sens: Priest of the fifteenth class during the time of David
Priest who returned with Zerubbabel after the exile
H1083H.detail:
1. Bilga is a priest who belonged to the fifteenth priestly class instituted during the time of King David. These classes were divisions of the priestly body allowing for a rotation of service at the temple (Nehemiah 12:5).
2. After returning from exile in Babylon, Bilga returned to Jerusalem with the governor Zerubbabel and participated in the restoration of worship. His name appears among the leaders of the priests who sealed the covenant of the people with God (Nehemiah 12:18).
H1083H.origine: The name Bilga literally means "glee" or "joy" in Hebrew. It is formed from a root evoking cheerfulness. This same person is sometimes called Bilgai (a variant of the same name). Several members of this priestly family bear the name, which shows the importance of lineage in temple service.
H1083H.emploi: Bilga is mentioned twice in the book of Nehemiah, both in the context of the return from exile and the organization of worship. The first mention lists the leaders of the priests who returned with Zerubbabel; the second, in chapter 12, again lists the priestly leaders and their successors, showing the continuity of temple service over several generations. Bilga represents the priestly class that ensured the continuity of Israel's religious life after the exile.

sens: Priest during the time of the captivity and the return from exile
H1084.detail: Bilgai is a priest who lived at the time of the return from exile, after the Babylonian captivity. He is among the priests who committed to the covenant with Nehemiah, in which the people renewed their commitment to God and His laws. His name appears in the official list of priests who sealed this solemn pact (Nehemiah 10:8).
H1084.origine: The name Bilgai means "my joy" or "my glee" in Hebrew (from the Hebrew "bilga" evoking rejoicing). It is a variant of the name Bilgah (בִּלְגָּה), which designates a family of priests mentioned elsewhere in the texts. The names of priests from this period often carried positive meanings, expressing trust in God and the faith of the people.
H1084.emploi: Bilgai is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:8, where he is listed among the priests who signed Nehemiah's covenant. This covenant, sealed after the return from exile, marked the Jewish people's recommitment to obey the Law of Moses and honor God. The presence of his name in this list underscores his role as a religious leader and his personal commitment to the spiritual restoration of Israel.
H1084.portee: The figure of Bilgai reminds us that the return from exile was not just a political or geographical return: it was a spiritual restoration. The priests, including Bilgai, led this renewal movement, showing that faith requires concrete and public commitments. This inspires the believer to also renew their covenant with God, not through vague words, but through a firm and witnessed act.

sens: One of the three friends of Job who came to comfort him in his suffering
H1085.detail: Bildad is one of the three companions of Job mentioned at the beginning of the book: he comes from the region of Shuh. Along with Eliphaz the Temanite and Zophar the Naamathite, he learns of the terrible trials that befall Job—ulcers, ruin, loss of his family—and consults with them to go and mourn and comfort him (Job 2:11). Throughout the book, Bildad intervenes three times to present his theology: he asserts that God always punishes sin and rewards righteousness, and that Job must have committed some hidden fault. His speeches are shorter and more systematic than those of Eliphaz. In the end, after God speaks to Job and rebukes him, Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar obey divine orders and offer sacrifices; God then accepts Job's prayer and restores him (Job 42:9).
H1085.origine: The name Bildad, in ancient Hebrew, literally means "confusion (or mixture) of love." It is an Aramaic name that may reflect the north-Mesopotamian origin of this character. Bildad represents a type of conventional wisdom from the patriarchal era.
H1085.emploi: Bildad appears five times in the book of Job. First introduced in Job 2:11 as one of the three friends who come to comfort Job, he then speaks three times: in Job 8:1, where he urges Job to turn to God because "God does not reject the blameless man"; in Job 18:1, where he develops his view of divine retribution; and finally in Job 25:1, his last speech. Each time, he seeks to convince Job that his suffering is the result of some sin. He reappears one last time in Job 42:9, where he obeys God and offers a sacrifice with the other two friends.
H1085.portee: Bildad symbolizes the temptation to judge too quickly and to theologize the suffering of others without true compassion. Although he presents himself as a friend, his veiled reproaches hurt Job instead of helping him. His example teaches the reader that true consolation does not consist of imposing our preconceived ideas, but in listening, recognizing the mystery of trials, and trusting God even when we do not understand.

sens: To undergo the wear of time, to become old
To cause something to wear out, to consume it
To fully enjoy something
H1086.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of time wearing and aging: a garment that wears out from being worn, a body that weakens and ages (Genesis 18:12: Sarah laughed, saying, "Now that I am old"). It is the image of something gradually losing its strength and integrity.
2. The verb can also mean to cause destruction or wear: the wicked who destroy the people (1 Chronicles 17:9), or in a physical sense, a garment that is consumed and falls to tatters (Isaiah 51:6: "The earth will wear out like a garment"). It is to wear something out to the point of annihilation.
3. In the context of relation to possessions or life, the word can take on a sense of complete enjoyment or exhaustion through satisfaction: not to destroy but to "wear out" in the sense of fully benefiting from it.
H1086.origine: The verb בָּלָה comes from a Hebrew-Aramaic root that paints the image of decline and disintegration: something that time and use gradually erode. The Aramaic shares the same root (בְּלָא). It is a word that evokes the natural process of wear, without an initial moral notion, but often metaphorically applied to the fragility of human things in the face of eternity.
H1086.emploi: The verb בָּלָה appears 14 times in the Old Testament, mainly in contexts where the wear of the body, clothing, or structures is described. Deuteronomy 29:5 mentions the clothing of the Israelites that did not wear out in the desert—a miracle showing divine protection. Psalms 102:27 and Isaiah 51:6 use it poetically to show how all created things wear out and perish, while God remains. Job 13:28 expresses the fear of the body that is consumed in decay. Nehemiah 9:21 celebrates again the fact that the clothing did not wear out. The word thus describes both a physical reality and a theological truth about the fragility of creatures.
H1086.portee: This word reminds the reader that everything created—clothing, bodies, empires, the earth itself—is subject to the wear of time and death. It is both a humility before reality and a call to fix one's gaze on what does not wear out: God and His justice. For the believer, this encourages not to place trust in perishable things, but in the eternal.

sens: That has served long, worn by use
That has lost its freshness, its solidity, damaged or patched up
Figuratively: one who has aged in a sinful conduct
H1087.detail:
1. The word describes objects, clothing, or shoes marked by time and use. This is the case with the bags, wineskins, and clothing of the Gibeonites in Joshua 9:4-5: worn travel items that give the impression of a long journey, which is part of their ruse to deceive Israel.

2. By extension, it designates what has deteriorated, broken, or been mended: the wineskins "torn and sewn back together," the shoes "repaired" are not only old but also imperfect and fragile.

3. Figuratively, the word applies to a person who has persisted long in a wrong path: in Ezekiel 23:43, the one who has "aged in adultery" means she has worn out, consumed by years of prostitution, becoming like a worn and degraded object.
H1087.origine: The Hebrew root describes progressive wear: what is ancient, now worn and tired. The word evokes the image of an object that has served long and whose strength is exhausted—like a garment that frays or a human who weakens with the years.
H1087.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in Joshua 9. Two uses describe the belongings of the Gibeonites as worn to lend credibility to their lie. The third use, in Ezekiel 23:43, transfers the image of physical wear to the moral and personal domain: a woman who has aged in adultery, meaning she has worn out, degraded by years of sinful conduct. The three uses retain the fundamental meaning: something or someone marked by time and wear.
H1087.portee: This word reminds us that sin gradually wears out and destroys those who indulge in it. Ezekiel does not merely describe a one-time act of wrongdoing, but the moral wear of a person who sinks into unfaithfulness: aging in guilt means consuming oneself from within. For the reader, this invites reflection on the destructive power of prolonged sin and the urgency of repentance.

sens: City in the territory of Simeon
H1088.detail: Bala is a city located in Israel, in the territory assigned to the tribe of Simeon during the division of the promised land. It is mentioned in the list of cities in the territory of Simeon (Joshua 19:3), alongside other localities such as Hazar-Shual and Atsem.
H1088.origine: The name literally means "has aged" or "wears out," perhaps evoking an ancient locality or a place that bears the marks of time. This type of designation may refer to ruins or an ancient settlement.
H1088.emploi: Bala appears only once in the Bible, in the list of cities in the territory of Simeon in Joshua 19:3. This enumeration is part of the account of the distribution of territory among the tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan. The context is purely geographical and administrative: it is about establishing the boundaries and cities belonging to each tribe.

sens: Rachel's maid
Jacob's concubine
Mother of Dan and Naphtali
H1090A.detail: Bilhah is a woman from the time of the Patriarchs, a servant whom Rachel gave to Jacob as a concubine. She first appears in Genesis 29:29, when Laban gives her to Rachel to accompany her. Rachel, having been barren for a long time, wants to have children through this servant: "She said: Here is my maid Bilhah; go to her; let her bear on my knees, and that I may also have children by her" (Genesis 30:3). Bilhah conceives and gives birth to two sons of Jacob: Dan and Naphtali (Genesis 30:5-7). Thus, she figures among the mothers of the twelve tribes of Israel. However, she also experiences shame: Reuben, Jacob's son by Leah, "went and lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine," an act that provoked Israel's anger (Genesis 35:22).
H1090A.origine: The name Bilhah means "troubled" or "confused" in Hebrew. It derives from a root that expresses agitation and disorder. This name carries something of the precarious condition of this woman: a servant without stable status, a concubine without the rights of a wife, she lives in an ambiguous and dependent situation. The patriarchal context in which she appears shows how women serving in those ancient times could be given in marriage and used for procreation, without having a say in these arrangements.
H1090A.emploi: Bilhah appears ten times in the Bible, all in Genesis and 1 Chronicles. She is first mentioned when she is given to Rachel (Genesis 29:29). The core of the uses concerns her motherhood: she is pregnant and gives birth twice for Jacob (Genesis 30:5 and 30:7), thus giving birth to two tribes (Dan and Naphtali). She appears in the genealogies of Jacob's sons (Genesis 35:25; 37:2; 46:25; 1 Chronicles 7:13). Finally, a crucial passage reports her humiliation: Reuben "went and lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine," which brought Israel's anger upon him (Genesis 35:22). Her role in the biblical story is thus that of a mother of the twelve tribes, but also of a vulnerable woman, a victim of the patriarchal order and the passions of the men around her.
H1090A.portee: Bilhah reminds us that the Bible does not hide the difficult and sometimes obscure realities of the lives of the patriarchs. Her story also shows how, in God's design, two of the twelve tribes of Israel—Dan and Naphtali—were born of a servant, which teaches the equal dignity of all the children of Israel before God, regardless of their mother's status. It invites the reader to see how God includes in the story of salvation people in humble and sometimes painful situations.

sens: city of the tribe of Simeon
H1090B.detail: Bilha is a city that belonged to the tribe of Simeon in Israel. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the list of cities of Simeon in 1 Chronicles 4:29, alongside other localities such as Etsem and Tholad.
H1090B.origine: The name Bilha means "troubled" or "confused" in Hebrew, probably referring to troubled or agitated waters. It is an ancient geographical name that designated a locality in the Israelite territory.
H1090B.emploi: Bilha appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:29, where it is listed among the cities of the territory of Simeon. This list reminds the exiled Israelites of the land inheritance that God had given to this tribe. Bilha was a minor city in the kingdom of Israel, the exact location of which is not identified with certainty today.

sens: Extreme fear, sudden fright that seizes someone
Event or force that causes this fright
Destruction or annihilation that occurs without warning
Sensation of being surrounded, pursued by fear
H1091.detail:
1. Terror is fear in its most intense form, one that paralyzes or overwhelms. Job says that terrors surround him like an army surrounds a city (Job 30:15), and that they surprise him like a flood (Job 27:20): one then lives in constant anguish.
2. The word also designates the dreadful event itself, that which provokes fright — sudden death that comes in an instant (Psalms 73:19), or the disaster that falls upon the wicked. Job will speak of the "king of terrors" (Job 18:14) as a power of destruction.
3. Sometimes the word emphasizes the unexpected and overwhelming nature of misfortune: an event that strikes without warning, which takes away a person's security and certainties. This is what makes terror so effective — it was not seen coming.
4. The common image is that of encirclement: terrors "surround" Job (Job 18:11), they encircle him, pressing him from all sides like an army around a city. It is the helplessness in the face of a danger that cannot be escaped.
H1091.origine: The word comes from the root בלל (see trouble, confusion), which refers to the idea of being disoriented, thrown into confusion. Terror is the state of mind of one who loses their bearings. In Hebrew, this word belongs to the family of terms that describe sudden destruction and annihilation: it is close to the vocabulary of falling and overturning.
H1091.emploi: This word appears about ten times in the Old Testament, especially in the poetic (Job, Psalms) and prophetic (Isaiah, Ezekiel) books. It is very present in Job, where it describes the anxieties and plagues that overwhelm the suffering righteous. In these texts, terror is often personified: it comes, it takes away, it grips. It can also designate a catastrophic event, a sudden destruction. In the prophets (notably Ezekiel), it characterizes the judgment that strikes peoples and kings.
H1091.portee: For the biblical reader, this word reminds us that extreme fear is a human reality, even for the righteous. But it also invites us not to remain prisoners of terror: in the Psalms, it is the adversary to confront, and trust in God is the response. The word finally emphasizes that God knows our anxieties and that He can deliver us if we turn to Him.

sens: Son of Ezer, a descendant of Esau
Leader or member of an Edomite clan
H1092G.detail:
1. Bilhan is a character from the patriarchal times, son of Ezer and brother of Zaavan and Akan. He appears in the genealogy of Esau in Genesis 36:27, where he is listed among the direct descendants of Ezer.

2. He represents an important Edomite lineage: Edomite clans often bore the name of their ancestors, and Bilhan figures as a leader or ancestor of a clan in the genealogies of Edom (Genesis 36:27 and 1 Chronicles 1:42), suggesting his foundational role in the history of Esau and his descendants.
H1092G.origine: The name means "their weakening" or "their decline" in Hebrew. It comes from a root expressing the idea of weakness or decay. Bilhan is simply a personal name without particular symbolic connotation in the biblical context; it is a patronymic that identifies a branch of Esau's family and gave its name to an Edomite clan.
H1092G.emploi: Bilhan appears only twice in the Bible, both times in genealogies: in Genesis 36:27 and in 1 Chronicles 1:42. These two passages list exactly the same ancestors and descendants, with 1 Chronicles reiterating and confirming the genealogy established in Genesis. He is a historical figure from the patriarchal times, belonging to Esau's line, with no particular action narrative related to him in the Scriptures.

sens: Benjamite, family leader during the Divided Monarchy
H1092H.detail: Bilhan is a man from the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned only once in the genealogies during the Divided Monarchy. He is the son of Jediael and the father of seven children: Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Kenaana, Zethan, Tarsis, and Achishachar (1 Chronicles 7:10). His name appears in the list of Benjaminite families, giving him a place in the genealogical history of Israel, even though few details are given about his personal life.
H1092H.origine: The name Bilhan literally means "their decline" or "their weakness" in Hebrew. Although it is a proper name, it reflects a common practice in Israel of giving children names that carry meaning, often related to the parents' situation or a particular event. This name, like many in biblical genealogies, carries a theological or personal significance that is now lost to us.
H1092H.emploi: Bilhan is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:10, in the genealogy of the sons of Benjamin. He appears as an important genealogical figure who produced a large offspring (seven sons are named). His presence in the genealogical records of the book of Chronicles underscores the importance of family lineages for the people of Israel, particularly during the time of the Divided Monarchy. No particular event of his life is recorded.

sens: Financial tribute collected by a sovereign state from the inhabitants or subjects of a territory
Forced contribution paid as tribute by a defeated people or one subordinate to a dominant political power
H1093.detail:
1. The tax is a tribute that the king or state collects from its subjects to finance administration and the public treasury. In the three occurrences in the book of Ezra, this term appears alongside "tribute" and "toll": these are different types of contributions that the inhabitants of a region must pay. In Ezra 4:13, the adversaries of the temple reconstruction in Jerusalem warn the king that if the city is rebuilt, its inhabitants will no longer pay this tax to the royal treasury. This is a statement of their fear: a restored Jerusalem would become too powerful and refuse to pay what it owes.
2. The tax can also express political subjugation: it is the contribution that defeated peoples or provinces pay to their conqueror. In Ezra 4:20, it is recalled that the former kings of Jerusalem were so powerful that the surrounding countries paid them taxes, tribute, and tolls — which shows the past power of Judah. The tax thus becomes the visible sign of one power's domination over another.
H1093.origine: This word comes from a Semitic root that expresses the idea of "payment" or "contribution." In Hebrew, the context of the three occurrences (the book of Ezra) shows that it is a common administrative practice in the Persian Empire, of which Judea was a province. The word specifically refers to the financial burden imposed by the central authority on its subjects.
H1093.emploi: The word appears three times in the Bible, all in the book of Ezra, written during the time of the return from exile under Persian rule. In Ezra 4:13, the enemies of the people fear that the reconstruction of the temple will embolden Jerusalem to refuse its taxes. In Ezra 4:20, it recalls the past glory of Judah, when neighboring nations paid it tribute and taxes. In Ezra 7:24, the Persian king Artaxerxes exempts the priests, Levites, and temple servants from any financial contribution. The word always denotes an official tax burden, never a private matter.
H1093.portee: This word reminds believers of the reality of earthly powers and their administrative structures. It shows how God allows His people to live under human authority, even foreign, and how He can alter the king's decrees to protect the service of His temple. This can encourage the believer to recognize that God remains sovereign even when His people are politically subjugated.

sens: piece of torn or worn fabric
ragged clothing or cloth
old and dilapidated remnant of something
H1094.detail:
1. The word refers to a piece of fabric in poor condition, torn or very worn by time. In Jeremiah 38:11, Ebed-Melech brings tattered cloths and old rags that he lowers to Jeremiah, who is imprisoned in a cistern: these rags will serve as padding to prevent the rope from hurting the prisoner when he is pulled up.
2. The word more broadly evokes anything old and dilapidated, any fabric reduced to rags. It is a concrete term to designate something that has lost its original use and is worth almost nothing in the eyes of people.
3. By extension, it represents what is worn to the limit, patched or destroyed by the wear of time — the image of something that has served its time.
H1094.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "worn" or "exhausted." It is related to the idea of something that no longer has strength, substance, or value, something that has degraded over time and use. The context of Jeremiah clearly shows how a useful object becomes waste when it can no longer serve its original purpose.
H1094.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the passage of Jeremiah 38:11-12 where the prophet Jeremiah is captive in a cistern. Ebed-Melech, an Ethiopian servant of the king, frees him by using tattered cloths that he places under the prisoner’s armpits so that the rope does not crush him. This detail reveals the practical kindness of Ebed-Melech's gesture: even with scraps, with refuse, he protects the life of an innocent.
H1094.portee: This word shows how God can use what seems worthless: discarded rags, old cloth become instruments of salvation. It reminds us that true wealth is not in beautiful appearances, and that even small resources, put to the service of love for one’s neighbor, become precious.

sens: Name given to Daniel by the Babylonian authorities
Another name for the prophet Daniel, used in his visions and at the court of Babylon
H1095.detail:
1. Belteshazzar is the name that the chief of the eunuchs of Nebuchadnezzar assigns to Daniel upon his deportation to Babylon (Daniel 1:7). It is a Babylonian name imposed on a young Israelite to mark his integration into the king's court.
2. This Babylonian name becomes Daniel's primary designation in his visions and his life at the Persian court: it is notably found in the accounts of end-times visions that carry his teaching (Daniel 10:1), where he is clearly identified as "Daniel, whom they called Belteshazzar."
H1095.origine: The Babylonian name Belteshazzar literally means "lord of the treasure of the captives" or "lord of the narrow treasure." It is a compound name reflecting the culture and religion of Babylon, imposed on Daniel to erase his Hebrew identity and integrate him into the imperial administration.
H1095.emploi: Belteshazzar appears only twice in the Bible according to the Segond 1910. The first occurrence (Daniel 1:7) marks the moment when Daniel receives this new name upon arriving in Babylon, signifying his status as a captive incorporated into royal service. The second occurrence (Daniel 10:1) shows him still referred to by this name at the end of his life, under the reign of the Persian king Cyrus, suggesting that this name endured and characterized his long existence in Babylon and beyond.

sens: One of the greatest prophets of Israel, deported to Babylon during the exile
The Babylonian name given to Daniel by King Nebuchadnezzar
A man gifted with the ability to interpret dreams and riddles
A trusted advisor in the Babylonian empire, then the Persian empire
H1096.detail:
1. Belteshazzar is the Babylonian name given to the Hebrew prophet Daniel during his deportation to Babylon with other young Israelites. It was King Nebuchadnezzar who imposed this new name on him, as seen in Daniel 4:8, where it is specified that the king calls him this "after the name of my god."

2. Daniel, nicknamed Belteshazzar, is remarkable for his extraordinary gift of interpreting dreams and riddles. The king consults him several times — notably to explain his dream in Daniel 4:9 and 4:18 — because he recognizes in him a superior spirit filled with the Spirit of God (Daniel 5:12).

3. Thanks to this wisdom and faithfulness, Belteshazzar becomes one of the highest authorities in the Babylonian empire: the king appoints him chief of the magicians and places him in a position of trust. This shows how God elevates and honors those who remain faithful to Him, even in a foreign and idolatrous land.

4. The prophecies of Belteshazzar contained in the book of Daniel are essential for understanding the events of the end times and God's plan for the history of the world. Ezekiel mentions him, praising him for his righteousness (Ezekiel 14:14).
H1096.origine: Belteshazzar is the Aramaic equivalent of the Hebrew name Daniel. In Aramaic, Belteshazzar literally means "lord of the treasure of the strait" (or "protected by Bel"), Bel being the supreme god of Babylon. This name was imposed on the young prophet to mark his integration into the Babylonian royal court and his allegiance to the king's worship.
H1096.emploi: Belteshazzar appears only in the book of Daniel (six times in Aramaic) and once in the book of Ezekiel (in Hebrew, in the form of Daniel). It is the official name by which King Nebuchadnezzar and his court call him. Daniel is consulted to interpret royal dreams — the dream of the tree in Daniel 4, the hand writing on the wall in Daniel 5 — and each time he demonstrates the wisdom and boldness of one who draws his strength from God alone. The contrast between this idolatrous Babylonian name and Daniel's unwavering faithfulness to his God is a key element of the book's testimony: even when clothed in a foreign name and under pressure, Daniel remains the instrument of divine revelation.
H1096.portee: Belteshazzar embodies the believer who remains faithful in the midst of a hostile and idolatrous culture. His story teaches that God can elevate and honor those who do not renounce their faith, even in the face of royal power and the seduction of honors. It is also a reminder that true prophets of God are recognizable by the accuracy of their words and their moral integrity, not by their social position or their acceptance by the powerful of the world.

sens: absence or deprivation of something
lack, defect or insufficiency
cessation or interruption of an action
nothingness, absolute void
that lasts without interruption
H1097.detail:
1. "Without" expresses the absence of a thing or the deprivation of what should be present: "If I have seen the poor lacking clothing" (Job 31:19) means that this man had no clothing to cover himself. This is the simplest idea: something is missing.
2. The word also denotes a lack or defect that leaves a person in insufficiency or distress: "None of his kin dwell in his tent" (Job 18:15) depicts complete isolation, the absence of any family support. This is a deprivation that leads to a dire consequence.
3. "Without" can mark the interruption or cessation of an action: "The oil has ceased to anoint them" (2 Samuel 1:21) means that the royal anointing has stopped, that it no longer takes place. The action has no continuation.
4. The word can denote nothingness or absolute void, the total absence of substance: "He hangs the earth upon nothing" (Job 26:7) expresses that beneath the earth there is nothing, complete emptiness.
5. "Without" is also used in the sense of "continuously" or "unceasingly": the absence of interruption, that which lasts without end.
H1097.origine: The Hebrew word בְּלִי (bli) comes from a root that evokes wear, the absence of duration, that which does not endure. This is why it fundamentally means "without." It belongs to a family of Hebrew words expressing absence and negation. The word marks what is not, what does not exist, or what does not continue. This root is very ancient and very common in biblical Hebrew.
H1097.emploi: The word הובשblí appears 57 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the poetic and prophetic books such as Job, Psalms, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. It primarily expresses the absence of necessities (clothing, food, water) in human distress: Job speaking of the misfortune of the wicked, the psalmists mentioning their needs. It also appears when the text describes emptiness or total absence ("upon nothing"), or the interruption of a blessing (the oil that ceases to anoint). The Segond translates it sometimes as "without," sometimes as "nothingness," "none," "cease," depending on whether the context emphasizes the absence of a thing, the void, or the stopping of an action. It is a common word, essential for expressing deprivation and negation.
H1097.portee: Understanding "without" helps to grasp how Scripture describes human suffering and need: the poor have "without" shelter, clothing, or food; the sinner finds himself "without" help. This shows that the Bible takes material and moral deprivations seriously. Conversely, when God acts, it is often to fill what is lacking and to fill the "nothingness." This word thus invokes compassion for those who have nothing and gratitude towards the One who provides.

sens: Coarse food given to domestic animals, especially draft animals
Grass or straw intended to feed livestock
H1098.detail: 1. Fodder is the food given to working animals such as oxen and donkeys. It is generally simple and coarse food: tender grass, straw, or crop residues. In Job 6:5, the wild donkey does not bray "near its fodder" as a well-fed domestic animal would, which shows that fodder is expected and recognized food. 2. The word also denotes the action of harvesting or gathering this food from the fields. In Job 24:6, the poor "cut the fodder that remains in the fields" after the harvest, using what is left to feed their animals. In Isaiah 30:24, the winnowed fodder with shovel and fan is prepared and cleaned fodder, ready to be distributed to the plowing animals.
H1098.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes food, nourishment. It specifically designates what is given to animals — common food, unrefined, such as straw or hay. It is a concrete word deeply rooted in the agricultural life of the ancient East.
H1098.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in wisdom or prophetic books (Job and Isaiah), and always in relation to the feeding of working animals. In Job 6:5, it contrasts with Job's miserable condition, who complains of being without food like an animal without fodder. In Job 24:6, it represents what the poor can glean. In Isaiah 30:24, it describes the future well-being of livestock in days of blessing: even salted fodder (thus of particular quality) will nourish the animals.
H1098.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not despise humble and earthly details: the food of draft animals has its place in Scripture. It invites the reader to see in the simplest creatures a creation of God that deserves care and attention.
